15413.m: Rousseau doubted the belief in progress of his time.

15414.q: In his Discourse on Inequality of 1755, what did Rousseau see as a main cause of inequality among people?
15414.e: For Rousseau the trouble began when someone fenced off a piece of land and said it belonged to him. In the state of nature people had been much more equal.
15414.m: Rousseau saw private property as a root of inequality.

15415.q: What is the central term in Rousseau's ‘Social Contract’ of 1762 for the will of the people directed at the common good?
15415.e: The general will is more than the sum of individual wills, which Rousseau calls ‘volonté de tous’. It is the basis of popular sovereignty.
15415.m: For Rousseau the general will is the basis of the state.

15416.q: With which famous sentence does the first chapter of Rousseau's ‘Social Contract’ begin?
a: ‘Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.’
15416.e: The sentence asks how rule can be justified. The saying about the wolf comes from the tradition that Hobbes referred to.
15416.m: In the ‘Social Contract’ Rousseau asks how rule can be legitimate.

15417.q: What happened to Rousseau's novel on education ‘Émile’ in his home town of Geneva in 1762?
a: It became required reading in schools
15417.e: Because of its religious views the Geneva authorities had ‘Émile’ and the ‘Social Contract’ burned. ‘Émile’ was also banned in Paris.
15417.m: In 1762 Geneva had Rousseau's books burned.

15418.q: On which island in today's canton of Bern did Rousseau spend a few weeks in 1765 that he described as especially happy?
a: St Peter's Island in Lake Biel
15418.e: After Rousseau had been driven out of Môtiers, he lived briefly on St Peter's Island in autumn 1765. He later described this time in ‘Reveries of the Solitary Walker’.
15418.m: Rousseau found a short happy time on St Peter's Island in Lake Biel.

15419.q: Which contradiction between his life and work is often held against Rousseau?
a: He wrote about education but gave his own children to a foundling home
He praised monarchy but fought in the revolution
He wrote against the theatre but ran an opera house
He called for inequality but lived in poverty
15419.e: Rousseau gave all five of his children to foundling homes. Even so, his ‘Émile’ became one of the most influential books on education.
15419.m: Rousseau's life partly contradicted his work.

15420.q: What honour did the French National Convention give Rousseau in 1794?
a: His remains were moved to the Panthéon
A statue of him was put up in Versailles
He was made king after his death
15420.e: The revolutionaries revered Rousseau as the intellectual father of popular sovereignty. Voltaire had already been moved to the Panthéon in 1791.
15420.m: The French Revolution honoured Rousseau with a tomb in the Panthéon.

15421.q: What is the task of the judiciary in the separation of powers?
a: It carries out laws and governs
15421.e: The judiciary is the judicial power. The legislature makes the laws and the executive carries them out.
15421.m: The judiciary is the power that administers justice.

15422.q: What is the main aim of the separation of powers?
a: To limit power and so secure citizens' freedom
To let the government decide faster
To reduce the number of officials
15422.e: If no single body unites all powers, it cannot abuse its power so easily. The separation of powers is a core principle of the rule of law.
15422.m: The separation of powers protects freedom by sharing out power.

15423.q: Which example belongs to the system of ‘checks and balances’ in the USA?
a: The President can veto laws passed by Congress
The President appoints all members of Congress
Congress elects the President every year
The people remove the judges every two years
15423.e: In the USA the powers are not only separated but also control each other. In turn, Congress can remove the President through impeachment.
15423.m: With ‘checks and balances’ the powers control each other.

15424.q: Which body forms the federal executive in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Council with seven members
15424.e: The Federal Council is the highest governing and executive authority. The National Council and the Council of States together form the Federal Assembly, the legislature.
15424.m: In Switzerland the Federal Council is the government.

15425.q: Where does the Federal Supreme Court, Switzerland's highest judicial authority, have its main seat?
15425.e: The Federal Supreme Court has its main seat in Lausanne; two divisions work in Lucerne. Being located away from Bern underlines its independence.
15425.m: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court sits in Lausanne.

15426.q: What is special about the separation of powers in Switzerland compared with countries with full constitutional review?
a: The Federal Supreme Court cannot strike down federal laws for being unconstitutional
The Federal Council can overturn rulings of the Federal Supreme Court
The people elect the federal judges directly
The Federal Assembly has no law-making power
15426.e: According to Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, federal laws are binding on the Federal Supreme Court even if they might contradict the constitution. This shows the strong position of parliament and the people.
15426.m: In Switzerland the courts must apply federal laws even if they might be unconstitutional.

15427.q: What is meant by the vertical separation of powers?
a: The division of responsibilities between the Confederation, cantons and municipalities
The separation of legislature, executive and judiciary
The separation of church and state
The division of parliament into two chambers
15427.e: In federalism power is divided between several levels of the state. The separation of the three classic powers, on the other hand, is called the horizontal separation of powers.
15427.m: Federalism divides power between several levels of the state.

15428.q: Why do people speak rather of an interlocking of powers in parliamentary systems such as Germany?
a: Because parliament elects the government and many ministers are also members of parliament
Because there are no courts there
Because the king exercises all powers
15428.e: The government and the parliamentary majority are closely linked, and control is mainly exercised by the opposition. The separation is therefore less strict than in the presidential system of the USA.
15428.m: In a parliamentary system government and parliament are closely intertwined.

15429.q: What did the English Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 guarantee?
15429.e: Anyone who is arrested must quickly be brought before a judge. The law is seen as an early protection against arbitrary state power.
15429.m: The Habeas Corpus Act protects against arbitrary imprisonment.

15430.q: Which English document of 1689 strengthened the rights of Parliament against the Crown after the Glorious Revolution?
15430.e: The Bill of Rights was passed by Parliament in December 1689. It set out, for example, the right of petition and limited the king's power.
15430.m: The Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the power of the English Crown.

15431.q: Which document of 12 June 1776 is considered one of the first modern declarations of human rights?
a: The Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen
15431.e: The Virginia Declaration of Rights declared all people to be equally free by nature. It also served as a model for the French declaration of 1789.
15431.m: The Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776 is an early declaration of human rights.

15432.q: When did the French National Assembly adopt the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen?
15432.e: The declaration was written shortly after the storming of the Bastille. The Marquis de Lafayette played a major part in drafting it.
15432.m: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen dates from August 1789.

15433.q: Who wrote the ‘Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen’ in 1791?
15433.e: Olympe de Gouges criticised that the declaration of 1789 did not include women. She called for equal rights for women.
15433.m: In 1791 Olympe de Gouges called for equal rights for women.

15434.q: How was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted in the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948?
a: With no votes against and 8 abstentions
By a narrow majority against 20 votes
Only by the five victorious powers
15434.e: 48 states voted for it, none against, and 8 abstained. The declaration has 30 articles, but as a resolution it is not legally binding.
15434.m: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948 with no votes against.

15435.q: Since when has the European Convention on Human Rights applied to Switzerland?
15435.e: The ECHR was signed in Rome in 1950, and Switzerland joined it in 1974. Complaints are decided by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
15435.m: Switzerland has been bound by the ECHR since 1974.

15436.q: Which rights belong to the so-called second generation of human rights?
a: Collective rights such as the right to peace
Rights of the nobility and the Church
15436.e: The first generation includes rights of protection such as freedom of expression, the second rights to benefits such as the right to education, the third collective rights. The division is disputed because it can suggest a ranking.
15436.m: The second generation includes social human rights such as the right to education.

15437.q: Which British law of 1765 required a tax on printed matter such as newspapers and documents in the colonies?
15437.e: The Stamp Act of 22 March 1765 taxed printed matter in the North American colonies. It caused fierce protests and was repealed as early as 1766.
15437.m: The Stamp Act of 1765 was one of the first big triggers of colonial resistance.

15438.q: Which principle summed up the colonists' protest against British taxes?
15438.e: The colonists argued that Parliament in London had no right to tax them because they had no members of their own there.
15438.m: The colonists did not want to pay taxes without their own representation in Parliament.

15439.q: What happened in the so-called Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770?
a: British soldiers shot several citizens in Boston
Colonists threw tea into the harbour
The British occupied the Massachusetts parliament
15439.e: On 5 March 1770 British soldiers fired into an angry crowd and killed five people. The Patriots made heavy use of the event for their propaganda.
15439.m: The Boston Massacre of 1770 became a powerful propaganda image against the British.

15440.q: What did the colonists protest against with the Boston Tea Party in 1773?
a: Against the British tea tax and the East India Company's tea monopoly
Against a British ban on drinking tea
Against French tea merchants in the harbour
Against dock workers' wages being too high
15440.e: On 16 December 1773 colonists disguised as Native Americans threw cargoes of East India Company tea into Boston Harbour.
15440.m: The Boston Tea Party of December 1773 was a protest against the British tea monopoly.

15441.q: How did the British Parliament react to the Boston Tea Party in 1774?
a: With the Intolerable Acts, which among other things closed Boston Harbour
By abolishing all taxes in the colonies
By inviting American members to London
15441.e: The punitive laws of spring 1774, known as the Intolerable Acts, closed Boston Harbour and restricted self-government in Massachusetts.
15441.m: The harsh punitive laws of 1774 drew the colonies closer together.

15442.q: With which skirmishes did the armed conflict begin on 19 April 1775?
15442.e: On 19 April 1775 the first shots were fired between British troops and colonial militias at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts.
15442.m: The War of Independence began in April 1775 at Lexington and Concord.

15443.q: Which pamphlet by Thomas Paine argued forcefully for independence in January 1776?
15443.e: Thomas Paine's ‘Common Sense’ appeared on 10 January 1776 and spread in huge numbers. It convinced many colonists that a break with the Crown was necessary.
15443.m: With ‘Common Sense’ Thomas Paine made the idea of independence popular.

15444.q: Why is the Battle of Saratoga in 1777 considered a turning point in the War of Independence?
a: The victory persuaded France to make an alliance with the Americans
Afterwards Canada and Florida joined the union
15444.e: After the British surrender at Saratoga in October 1777, France made an alliance with the United States on 6 February 1778.
15444.m: The victory at Saratoga won the Americans France as an ally.

15445.q: Which surrender of British troops in October 1781 practically decided the war?
15445.e: On 19 October 1781 General Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown to American and French troops.
15445.m: With the surrender at Yorktown in 1781 the war was decided militarily.

15446.q: In which peace treaty did Great Britain recognise the independence of the USA in 1783?
15446.e: The Peace of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783. In it Great Britain recognised the United States as an independent state.
15446.m: Only the Peace of Paris in 1783 sealed US independence in international law.

15447.q: Which French nobleman fought as a young general alongside Washington and later also played a role in the French Revolution?
15447.e: Lafayette served as a volunteer in the Continental Army and became a close confidant of Washington. In 1789 he put forward a draft for the declaration of human rights.
15447.m: Lafayette linked the American and the French Revolutions.

15448.q: When was the Constitution of the United States adopted by the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia?
15448.e: The Constitutional Convention adopted the Constitution on 17 September 1787. It came into force in 1789 after ratification by the states.
15448.m: The US Constitution of 1787 is considered the oldest written national constitution still in force.

15449.q: On which day did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
15449.e: The Continental Congress adopted the text on 4 July 1776. This day is now the national holiday of the USA.
15449.m: 4 July 1776 is seen as the birthday of the United States.

15450.q: Who wrote most of the text of the Declaration of Independence?
15450.e: Thomas Jefferson of Virginia wrote the draft on behalf of a committee of five. Adams and Franklin changed little; Congress then cut the text by about a quarter.
15450.m: Thomas Jefferson is the main author of the Declaration of Independence.

15451.q: Who did NOT belong to the ‘Committee of Five’ that prepared the Declaration?
15451.e: The committee was made up of Jefferson, Adams, Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. At that time Washington was leading the army.
15451.m: Washington was not on the committee because he commanded the Continental Army.

15452.q: Which king ruled Great Britain when the American colonies declared independence in 1776?
15452.e: George III reigned from 1760 to 1820. The Declaration of Independence portrays him as a tyrant.
15452.m: The USA declared independence from King George III in 1776.

15453.q: How many British colonies declared their independence together in 1776?
15453.e: The 13 colonies on the east coast of North America broke away from Great Britain together. The 13 stripes of the US flag recall this.
15453.m: 13 colonies founded the United States in 1776.

15454.q: Which rights does the preamble expressly name as ‘unalienable’?
a: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
15454.e: The Declaration names ‘Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness’ as examples of the unalienable rights of all people.
15454.m: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness as basic rights.

15455.q: Which philosopher's teaching on natural rights and the consent of the governed shaped the preamble especially strongly?
15455.e: Locke's idea that governments derive their power from the consent of the governed and must protect natural rights is at the heart of the preamble.
15455.m: John Locke's theory of natural law forms the foundation of the Declaration of Independence.

15456.q: Against whom is the long list of charges in the main part of the Declaration mainly directed?
15456.e: The main part lists accusations against King George III in order to portray him as a tyrant and justify the break.
15456.m: The Declaration justifies the separation with charges against the king.

15457.q: How many delegates signed the Declaration of Independence?
15457.e: The Declaration bears the signatures of 56 delegates. Most signed the official copy on 2 August 1776.
15457.m: A total of 56 delegates signed the Declaration.

15458.q: Which contradiction in the Declaration is discussed especially critically by historians?
a: It proclaims the equality of all people while slavery continued
It was only published in French
It declared the king to be president
15458.e: Many signatories, including Jefferson, owned enslaved people. In practice the formula of equality did not apply to the enslaved, women and Indigenous people.
15458.m: For a long time the formula of equality of 1776 did not apply to everyone.

15459.q: Where is the original of the Declaration of Independence kept today?
a: In the National Archives in Washington, D.C.
In the British Museum in London
In the Library of Congress in Philadelphia
15459.e: The parchment is on display in the National Archives in Washington, D.C., together with the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.
15459.m: The original Declaration is in the National Archives in Washington.

15460.q: In which colony was George Washington born in 1732?
15460.e: Washington was born on 22 February 1732 in Westmoreland County in the colony of Virginia.
15460.m: George Washington came from a planter family in Virginia.

15461.q: In which war did Washington gain his first military experience before the revolution?
a: In the French and Indian War
In the War of the Spanish Succession
15461.e: From 1754 Washington led Virginia militias against the French, for example at Fort Necessity, and in 1755 took part in Braddock's expedition.
15461.m: Washington learned the art of war in the French and Indian War.

15462.q: When did the Continental Congress appoint Washington commander-in-chief of the Continental Army?
15462.e: On 15 June 1775, on John Adams's proposal, Congress unanimously chose Washington as commander-in-chief. At the beginning of July 1775 he took command near Boston.
15462.m: Washington became commander-in-chief of the Continental Army in June 1775.

15463.q: Which surprise attack after crossing the Delaware raised the army's morale at the end of 1776?
15463.e: On the night of 25 to 26 December 1776 Washington's troops crossed the Delaware and defeated the Hessian soldiers at Trenton.
15463.m: The victory at Trenton at the end of 1776 gave the almost beaten army new courage.

15464.q: What does Valley Forge stand for in the history of the War of Independence?
a: For the Continental Army's harsh winter camp of 1777/78
For the place of the Declaration of Independence
15464.e: In the winter camp at Valley Forge the soldiers suffered from cold, hunger and disease. An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 men died, but the army was retrained there.
15464.m: Valley Forge stands for the army holding out in the winter of 1777/78.

15465.q: What did Washington preside over in Philadelphia in 1787?
15465.e: Washington was unanimously elected president of the Constitutional Convention, which met from May to September 1787.
15465.m: In 1787 Washington led the convention that drew up the US Constitution.

15466.q: When did Washington take office as the first President of the USA?
15466.e: Washington took the oath of office on 30 April 1789 at Federal Hall in New York.
15466.m: George Washington became the first President of the United States in 1789.

15467.q: Which precedent did Washington set when he declined a third term in 1796?
a: The limit of two terms became a tradition
From then on presidents were appointed by the king
Presidents had to come from Virginia
15467.e: Washington voluntarily left office in 1797 after two terms. This tradition held until Franklin D. Roosevelt and was written into the 22nd Amendment in 1951.
15467.m: Washington's voluntary retirement founded the tradition of at most two terms.

15468.q: Among other things, what did Washington warn against in his Farewell Address of 1796?
a: Party strife and permanent alliances with foreign powers
15468.e: In the Farewell Address of 19 September 1796 Washington urged unity, warned against factions and advised restraint towards permanent alliances.
15468.m: Washington's Farewell Address urged unity and restraint in foreign policy.

15469.q: How did Washington deal in his will with the people he had enslaved?
a: He ordered the freeing of the enslaved people who belonged directly to him
He left them all to his nephews
He sold them all before his death
15469.e: Washington's will provided for the freeing of the 124 enslaved people he owned himself, most of them only after his wife's death; Martha freed them in 1801. The other enslaved people at Mount Vernon belonged to the estate from Martha's first marriage and remained unfree.
15469.m: Washington owned enslaved people and only ordered some of them freed in his will.

15470.q: Where did George Washington die in 1799?
15470.e: Washington died on 14 December 1799 at Mount Vernon in Virginia and was also buried there.
15470.m: George Washington died in 1799 at his estate Mount Vernon.

15471.q: What main cause forced Louis XVI to summon the Estates-General in 1788?
a: The death of the heir to the throne
15471.e: France was heavily in debt, partly because of wars, including its support for the Americans. Reforms failed because of the resistance of the privileged.
15471.m: The state's financial crisis was the direct trigger of the revolution.

15472.q: When were the Estates-General opened in Versailles?
15472.e: The assembly of the three estates met in Versailles on 5 May 1789, for the first time since 1614.
15472.m: In May 1789 the Estates-General met again for the first time in 175 years.

15473.q: What did the deputies of the Third Estate swear in the tennis court on 20 June 1789?
a: Not to separate until France had a constitution
To obey the king without conditions
15473.e: After being locked out of their meeting hall, the deputies gathered in the tennis court and swore to draw up a constitution.
15473.m: With the Tennis Court Oath the deputies stood up against the king.

15474.q: What was decided in the August Decrees on the night of 4 to 5 August 1789?
a: The introduction of the revolutionary calendar
15474.e: In a stormy night session the nobility and clergy gave up many privileges. The National Assembly declared the feudal system abolished.
15474.m: The August Decrees of 1789 ended the feudal order in France.

15475.q: What did the women of Paris achieve with their march on Versailles in October 1789?
a: The royal family had to move to Paris
15475.e: On 5 October 1789 thousands of women marched to Versailles because of the bread shortage. The next day the royal family was taken to Paris, to the Tuileries.
15475.m: The women's march brought the king to Paris in October 1789.

15476.q: How was the royal family's attempt to escape stopped in June 1791?
a: They were recognised at Varennes and brought back
They reached Vienna and returned of their own accord
They were arrested at the Swiss border
They were discovered on a ship in Calais
15476.e: On the night of 20 to 21 June 1791 the family fled but was recognised at Varennes. After that trust in the king was badly shaken.
15476.m: The failed flight to Varennes destroyed trust in the king.

15477.q: Which form of state did the constitution of September 1791 lay down?
15477.e: The constitution of 1791 kept the king in office but bound him to the constitution and gave him only a suspensive veto.
15477.m: The first French constitution of 1791 created a constitutional monarchy.

15478.q: On whom did France declare war on 20 April 1792?
a: The King of Bohemia and Hungary, that is, Austria
15478.e: The National Assembly declared war on the Habsburg Francis II as King of Bohemia and Hungary. This began the Wars of the Coalitions.
15478.m: The Revolutionary Wars began with the declaration of war on Austria in 1792.

15479.q: What happened to many Swiss Guards during the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August 1792?
a: They were killed defending the king
They all went over to the revolutionaries
15479.e: Hundreds of Swiss Guards died in the attack on the Tuileries Palace. Since 1821 the Lion Monument in Lucerne has commemorated them.
15479.m: The Lion Monument in Lucerne commemorates the Swiss Guards killed in 1792.

15480.q: What consequence did the French Revolution have for Switzerland in 1798?
a: French troops invaded and the Helvetic Republic was created
Switzerland joined the Holy Roman Empire
Switzerland got its present Federal Constitution
15480.e: In 1798 French troops occupied the Old Swiss Confederacy. Under French influence the centralised Helvetic Republic was created.
15480.m: With the Helvetic Republic of 1798 the Revolution also reached Switzerland.

15481.q: Which song was written in 1792 as a war song and later became France's national anthem?
15481.e: Rouget de Lisle wrote the song in Strasbourg in 1792. It got its name from volunteers from Marseille who sang it in Paris.
15481.m: La Marseillaise was written in 1792 as a war song of the Revolution.

15482.q: Who made up the First Estate in pre-revolutionary France?
15482.e: The First Estate was made up of the clergy. It owned land and collected the tithe.
15482.m: In the Ancien Régime the clergy formed the First Estate.

15483.q: How could rich commoners rise into the nobility in the Ancien Régime?
a: By being elected in the village
By serving as an ordinary soldier
15483.e: Many high offices in the courts and administration could be bought and came with a noble title. This nobility of office was called the noblesse de robe.
15483.m: In the Ancien Régime you could rise into the nobility by buying offices.

15484.q: Roughly what share of France's population belonged to the Third Estate before 1789?
15484.e: The Third Estate included townspeople, craftsmen, workers and above all peasants. It made up over 95 per cent of the population.
15484.m: The great majority of the French belonged to the Third Estate.

15485.q: Which privilege did the clergy and nobility largely enjoy before 1789?
a: Exemption from the most important direct tax
The sole right to vote for women
The right not to obey any laws
15485.e: The first two estates were largely exempt from the taille, the most important direct tax. The tax burden fell mainly on the Third Estate.
15485.m: In the Ancien Régime the tax burden lay mainly on the Third Estate.

15486.q: Roughly what share of the French population lived as peasants before 1789?
15486.e: France was an agricultural country. About four fifths of the population were peasants, often burdened with dues to landlords, Church and state.
15486.m: Most people in pre-revolutionary France were peasants.

15487.q: What was the tithe that peasants had to pay in the Ancien Régime?
a: A customs fee at the border
15487.e: The tithe was a payment to the Church, originally a tenth of the harvest. It was abolished in 1789.
15487.m: The tithe was a payment by the peasants to the Church.

15488.q: Who wrote the pamphlet ‘What Is the Third Estate?’ at the beginning of 1789?
15488.e: Abbé Sieyès was himself a clergyman but defended the Third Estate in the pamphlet. It became one of the most influential pamphlets of the Revolution.
15488.m: With his pamphlet Abbé Sieyès provided the programme of the Third Estate.

15489.q: How did Sieyès answer the title question ‘What is the Third Estate?’ in his pamphlet?
15489.e: Sieyès wrote that the Third Estate was everything. Until now it had been nothing politically and now demanded to become something.
15489.m: For Sieyès the Third Estate was everything, but so far nothing politically.

15490.q: Why did the Third Estate demand voting by head instead of by estate in 1789?
a: Because in voting by estate it could always be outvoted by the clergy and nobility
Because the nobility had more deputies
Because the Church had no vote
15490.e: In voting by estate each estate had one vote, so the clergy and nobility could outvote the Third Estate two to one. Yet the Third Estate had twice as many deputies as each of the other estates.
15490.m: Voting by head would have given the Third Estate more weight.

15491.q: What did the deputies of the Third Estate declare themselves to be on 17 June 1789?
15491.e: The Third Estate declared that it represented the nation and called itself the National Assembly. This began the political revolution.
15491.m: As the National Assembly the Third Estate claimed to represent the whole nation.

15492.q: What is the political and social order of France before 1789 called?
15492.e: The term ‘Ancien Régime’, meaning old order, refers to the absolutist society of estates before the Revolution.
15492.m: The order before 1789 is called the Ancien Régime.

15493.q: On which date was the Bastille stormed?
15493.e: On 14 July 1789 Parisian insurgents stormed the fortress in the east of the city.
15493.m: The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became the symbol of the Revolution.

15494.q: Which dismissal by the king triggered the unrest in Paris before 14 July?
a: The dismissal of the finance minister Jacques Necker
The dismissal of the Archbishop of Paris
15494.e: Louis XVI dismissed the popular Necker on 11 July 1789. The news reached Paris on 12 July and caused great outrage.
15494.m: Necker's dismissal in July 1789 brought Paris to the boil.

15495.q: What did the Bastille stand for in the eyes of many Parisians?
a: The arbitrary power of the absolute monarchy
15495.e: The Bastille served as a state prison where people could be locked up without trial on the king's orders.
15495.m: The Bastille was seen as a symbol of royal arbitrary power.

15496.q: How many prisoners were still in the Bastille on 14 July 1789?
15496.e: Only seven prisoners were freed, including four forgers. The symbolic importance was much greater than the practical one.
15496.m: Only seven prisoners were freed when the Bastille was stormed.

15497.q: What happened to the governor of the Bastille, Bernard-René de Launay?
a: He was killed by the crowd
He was made general of the National Guard
15497.e: After the surrender de Launay was seized and killed by the angry crowd on the way to the town hall.
15497.m: The governor of the Bastille did not survive 14 July 1789.

15498.q: Who partly defended the Bastille on 14 July 1789?
15498.e: The fortress was defended by around 114 men: 82 invalid veterans and 32 Swiss grenadiers of the Salis-Samade regiment.
15498.m: The defenders of the Bastille included Swiss mercenaries.

15499.q: Roughly how many attackers died in the storming of the Bastille?
15499.e: The sources give around 94 to 98 attackers killed; the defenders had far fewer dead.
15499.m: The storming of the Bastille cost about a hundred attackers their lives.

15500.q: What happened to the fortress after it was stormed?
a: It was turned into a royal palace
It still stands today as a museum
It became the seat of the National Assembly
15500.e: The businessman Pierre-François Palloy had the Bastille taken down and sold its stones as souvenirs. Today the Place de la Bastille recalls it.
15500.m: The Bastille was completely demolished after it was stormed.

15501.q: What is the square in Paris where the Bastille used to stand called?
15501.e: After the fortress was demolished a square was created in its place. Today the July Column stands there.
15501.m: The Place de la Bastille recalls the stormed fortress.

15502.q: Which militia was formed in Paris in connection with the storming of the Bastille and commanded by Lafayette?
15502.e: In July 1789 the Paris middle class organised a citizens' militia, which was placed under Lafayette's command as the National Guard.
15502.m: The National Guard was formed in 1789 as the armed citizens' militia of Paris.

15504.q: Which event came a few weeks before the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in summer 1789?
15504.e: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789, and the Declaration followed on 26 August 1789. It consists of a preamble and 17 articles.
15504.m: The Declaration of human rights followed shortly after the storming of the Bastille.

15505.q: What does Article 1 of the Declaration of 1789 say?
a: People are born and remain free and equal in rights
The king is appointed by God
All citizens must do military service
The Catholic religion is the state religion
15505.e: Article 1 declares freedom and equality before the law to be birthrights. Social differences are only allowed if they serve the common good.
15505.m: Article 1 declares all people free and equal in rights from birth.

15506.q: Which natural rights does Article 2 of the Declaration of 1789 name?
a: Liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression
Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
15506.e: Article 2 names the protection of liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression as the purpose of every political association.
15506.m: Article 2 protects liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression.

15507.q: According to Article 3 of the Declaration, with whom does sovereignty lie?
15507.e: Article 3 states that all sovereignty comes from the nation. No person may exercise power that does not come from it.
15507.m: The Declaration of 1789 made the nation the holder of sovereignty.

15508.q: Which text of 1776 was one of the models for the French Declaration?
15508.e: The Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776 and the American Declaration of Independence inspired the authors in Paris.
15508.m: The French Declaration built on American texts on basic rights.

15510.q: Which argument did Olympe de Gouges make in Article 10 of her declaration?
a: If a woman may mount the scaffold, she must also be allowed to mount the speaker's platform
Women should only work within the family
Only married women should be allowed to vote
15510.e: De Gouges pointed out that women were fully responsible under criminal law but had no political rights.
15510.m: Olympe de Gouges linked equal duties with the demand for equal rights.

15511.q: How did Olympe de Gouges's life end?
a: She was executed on the guillotine in 1793
She became a minister of the republic
She died at a great age in Paris in 1830
15511.e: Olympe de Gouges was condemned for her criticism of the Jacobins and executed on 3 November 1793.
15511.m: Olympe de Gouges became a victim of the Reign of Terror in 1793.

15512.q: Which groups were excluded from full political rights in 1789 despite the formula of equality?
a: Women, enslaved people and men without enough property
15512.e: The constitution of 1791 distinguished active citizens with the vote from passive citizens without it. Women got no vote, and slavery remained in the colonies for the time being.
15512.m: Politically, the equality of 1789 at first applied only to part of the population.

15513.q: What importance does the Declaration of 1789 have in French law today?
a: Through the preamble of the 1958 constitution it is part of constitutional law
It applies only in the overseas territories
15513.e: The preamble of the constitution of the Fifth Republic of 4 October 1958 refers to the Declaration of 1789. It therefore still counts as constitutional law.
15513.m: The Declaration of human rights of 1789 is still part of the French constitution today.

15514.q: On which day did the newly elected National Convention abolish the monarchy?
15514.e: On 21 September 1792 the National Convention unanimously decided to abolish the monarchy. This began the First French Republic.
15514.m: The First French Republic began in September 1792.

15515.q: How was the National Convention elected in 1792?
15515.e: For the election of the National Convention in September 1792, universal suffrage for men, regardless of wealth, applied for the first time. Turnout, however, was very low.
15515.m: The National Convention of 1792 was elected by universal male suffrage.

15516.q: Which battle of 20 September 1792 saved the young republic from the Prussian troops?
15516.e: At Valmy French revolutionary troops under Dumouriez and Kellermann stopped the Prussian advance. The success boosted the Revolution at the decisive moment.
15516.m: The Cannonade of Valmy secured the survival of the Revolution in 1792.

15517.e: The National Convention sentenced the former king to death as ‘citizen Louis Capet’. He was guillotined in Paris on 21 January 1793.
15517.m: Louis XVI died on the guillotine in January 1793.

15518.q: Where did the counting of years in the revolutionary calendar begin?
a: With the start of the republic in September 1792
With the storming of the Bastille
15518.e: The revolutionary calendar, introduced in 1793, counted from 22 September 1792 as Year I of the Republic. It was meant to replace the Christian calendar.
15518.m: The revolutionary calendar began with Year I of the Republic in 1792.

15519.q: Which month names were typical of the revolutionary calendar?
a: Names from nature and weather such as Thermidor and Brumaire
Names of saints such as Peter and Paul
Names of revolutionaries such as Danton
15519.e: The months were named after the seasons and nature, for example Brumaire for fog or Thermidor for heat.
15519.m: The months of the revolutionary calendar have names from nature and weather.

15520.q: What happened to the Jacobin constitution of 1793?
a: It was adopted but never came into force
It became the model for the Swiss constitution of 1848
It was signed by the king
15520.e: The democratic constitution of 1793 was suspended because of war and crisis. Instead the Convention ruled with emergency powers.
15520.m: The constitution of 1793 stayed on paper and was never applied.

15521.q: Who led the executive of the republic from 1795?
15521.e: The constitution of 1795 created the Directory with five directors. It governed until 1799.
15521.m: From 1795 to 1799 the Directory governed France.

15522.q: With which event did Napoleon Bonaparte take power on 9 November 1799?
a: With the storming of the Tuileries
15522.e: On 18 Brumaire of Year VIII Bonaparte overthrew the Directory. He became First Consul in the Consulate.
15522.m: The coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 ended the actual revolutionary period.

15523.q: What did the National Convention decide for the French colonies on 4 February 1794?
15523.e: Under the impact of the slave revolt in Saint-Domingue, the Convention abolished slavery in 1794. Napoleon reintroduced it in 1802.
15523.m: The republic abolished slavery in 1794; Napoleon reintroduced it in 1802.

15524.q: When did the First French Republic formally end?
a: With the founding of the Empire in 1804
With the Congress of Vienna in 1815
With the fall of Louis XVI in 1792
15524.e: On 18 May 1804 Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor of the French, and the coronation followed on 2 December 1804. This ended the First Republic.
15524.m: In 1804 the First Republic gave way to Napoleon's Empire.

15525.q: Roughly what period does the Reign of Terror cover?
15525.e: Its start is dated differently, often to the summer of 1793 or to 5 September 1793. The Reign of Terror ended with Robespierre's fall on 27 July 1794.
15525.m: The Reign of Terror lasted from summer 1793 to summer 1794.

15526.q: Which body became the real centre of power during the Reign of Terror?
15526.e: The Committee of Public Safety, elected in April 1793, received sweeping powers and directed government, war and persecution.
15526.m: The Committee of Public Safety was the centre of power of the Reign of Terror.

15527.q: Which politician, nicknamed ‘the Incorruptible’, shaped the Reign of Terror?
15527.e: Robespierre, a lawyer from Arras and leader of the Jacobins, joined the Committee of Public Safety in July 1793.
15527.m: Robespierre was called ‘the Incorruptible’ because of his strict principles.

15528.q: What did the Law of Suspects of 17 September 1793 make possible?
a: Election of judges by the people
15528.e: The law defined ‘suspects’ very broadly. During the Reign of Terror around 300,000 people were arrested in total, often without concrete proof of any crime.
15528.m: The Law of Suspects made suspicion alone a reason for arrest.

15529.q: Who murdered the radical journalist Jean-Paul Marat in July 1793?
15529.e: Charlotte Corday, a sympathiser of the Girondins, stabbed Marat in his bath on 13 July 1793. She was executed shortly afterwards.
15529.m: Charlotte Corday killed the revolutionary Marat in 1793.

15530.q: When was Queen Marie Antoinette executed?
15530.e: After a trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal, Marie Antoinette was guillotined on 16 October 1793.
15530.m: Marie Antoinette died on the guillotine in October 1793.

15531.q: Which well-known revolutionary was executed on 5 April 1794 after calling for an end to the Terror?
15531.e: Danton and his followers, the ‘Indulgents’, were condemned and guillotined at the instigation of the Committee of Public Safety.
15531.m: In 1794 Danton fell victim to the Terror he had helped to build.

15532.q: According to the study by historian Donald Greer, how many death sentences were officially carried out during the Reign of Terror?
15532.e: Greer counted 16,594 death sentences carried out. Including deaths in prison and without trial, the total is estimated at at least 35,000 victims.
15532.m: The Reign of Terror claimed tens of thousands of lives.

15533.q: Which court sentenced thousands of people to death in Paris during the Reign of Terror?
15533.e: The Revolutionary Tribunal judged alleged enemies of the Revolution. In summer 1794 trials were shortened so much that a defence was hardly possible.
15533.m: The Revolutionary Tribunal was the tool of the Reign of Terror.

15534.q: Which religious festival did Robespierre have celebrated in Paris on 8 June 1794?
a: The Festival of the Supreme Being
The Festival of the Goddess Reason
15534.e: With the Cult of the Supreme Being Robespierre wanted to create a state religion based on reason. Many opponents saw it as arrogance.
15534.m: With the Festival of the Supreme Being Robespierre attempted a new state religion.

15535.q: How did the Reign of Terror end in July 1794?
a: The Convention overthrew Robespierre on 9 Thermidor and had him executed
The king returned to the throne
15535.e: On 27 July 1794 the Convention ordered Robespierre's arrest. On 28 July 1794 he was guillotined without trial together with close followers such as Saint-Just.
15535.m: Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor ended the Reign of Terror.

15536.q: In which town was Napoleon Bonaparte born on 15 August 1769?
15536.e: Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio on Corsica. Corsica had passed from Genoa to France only shortly before.
15536.m: Napoleon came from Ajaccio on Corsica.

15537.q: At which siege did the young artillery officer Napoleon make a name for himself in December 1793?
15537.e: The port of Toulon, held by royalists and the British, was recaptured on 19 December 1793. Napoleon's artillery plan contributed greatly and earned him promotion to brigadier general.
15537.m: Napoleon's rise began with the recapture of Toulon in 1793.

15538.q: What happened on 18 Brumaire of Year VIII, that is, 9 November 1799?
a: Napoleon overthrew the Directory in a coup
15538.e: The coup of 18 Brumaire overthrew the Directory and brought Napoleon to power as First Consul.
15538.m: On 18 Brumaire 1799 Napoleon took power in a coup.

15539.q: Which office did Napoleon take on after the coup of 1799?
15539.e: The constitution of the Consulate made Napoleon First Consul with sweeping powers. He only became emperor in 1804.
15539.m: From 1799 to 1804 Napoleon ruled as First Consul.

15540.q: How did Napoleon have his appointment as consul for life confirmed in 1802?
a: By being anointed by the Pope
By an election of the Estates-General
By a decision of the Directory
15540.e: After a referendum Napoleon was declared consul for life on 2 August 1802. Such plebiscites gave his rule the appearance of the people's approval.
15540.m: Napoleon used referendums to legitimise his power.

15541.q: What was special about the imperial coronation on 2 December 1804 in Notre-Dame de Paris?
a: Napoleon placed the crown on his own head
The Pope crowned him in Rome
The coronation took place in Reims
15541.e: Pope Pius VII was present, but Napoleon crowned himself. In this way he showed that he did not owe his power to the Church.
15541.m: In 1804 Napoleon crowned himself emperor in Notre-Dame.

15542.q: Which law code issued in 1804 unified civil law in France and had a lasting effect in many European countries?
15542.e: The Code civil of 1804 guaranteed, among other things, equality before the law for men and the protection of property. It influenced the law of many states, including western Switzerland.
15542.m: The Code civil of 1804 is seen as Napoleon's most lasting reform.

15543.q: With which pope did Napoleon make a concordat in 1801?
15543.e: After the Church conflicts of the Revolution, the Concordat of 1801 with Pius VII reset the relationship between France and the Catholic Church.
15543.m: With the Concordat of 1801 Napoleon reconciled the state with the Catholic Church.

15544.q: Which decoration did Napoleon found in 1802?
15544.e: The Légion d'honneur was founded in 1802 to honour civil and military merit. It is still France's highest decoration today.
15544.m: The Legion of Honour goes back to Napoleon in 1802.

15545.q: Whom did Napoleon marry as his second wife in 1810?
15545.e: After divorcing Joséphine, whom he had married in 1796, Napoleon married the emperor's daughter Marie Louise in 1810. He wanted an heir to the throne and a link with the House of Habsburg.
15545.m: His marriage to Marie Louise linked Napoleon with the Habsburgs in 1810.

15546.q: Which title did Napoleon's son receive at his birth in 1811?
15546.e: Napoleon II, the son of Napoleon and Marie Louise, received the title King of Rome. He was meant to continue the Bonaparte dynasty.
15546.m: From his birth in 1811 Napoleon's son bore the title King of Rome.

15547.q: Which of Napoleon's brothers became King of Spain in 1808?
15547.e: Joseph had previously been King of Naples and became King of Spain in 1808. Napoleon put relatives on thrones to secure his power in Europe.
15547.m: Napoleon secured his rule by making his brothers kings.

15548.q: Which famous find was made in 1799 during Napoleon's expedition to Egypt?
15548.e: In 1799 French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone with the same text in three scripts. It later made it possible to decipher hieroglyphs.
15548.m: The Rosetta Stone was discovered during Napoleon's expedition to Egypt.

15549.q: To which island was Napoleon exiled after his abdication in April 1814?
15549.e: After abdicating at Fontainebleau in April 1814, Napoleon was given the island of Elba off the Italian coast as a principality. From there he returned to France in 1815.
15549.m: Napoleon's first exile was the island of Elba in 1814.

15550.q: Where did Napoleon die on 5 May 1821?
a: On St Helena in the South Atlantic
15550.e: After Waterloo the British exiled Napoleon to the remote island of St Helena. He died there in 1821 at Longwood House.
15550.m: Napoleon died in exile on St Helena in 1821.

15551.q: Where were Napoleon's remains moved to in 1840?
15551.e: In 1840 Napoleon's remains were brought from St Helena to Paris. His tomb is in Les Invalides.
15551.m: Since 1840 Napoleon's tomb has been in Les Invalides in Paris.

15552.q: Why should historians read the ‘Bulletins of the Grande Armée’ critically?
a: They were written by his enemies
They were only written a hundred years later
15552.e: The bulletins were official war reports that stressed victories and played down losses. Anyone using them as a source must consider their purpose and author.
15552.m: Napoleon's official war reports are mainly propaganda sources.

15553.q: Which peace ended the war between France and Austria in the War of the First Coalition in 1797?
15553.e: After Napoleon's successes in Italy, France and Austria made the Treaty of Campo Formio on 17 October 1797. Austria gave up, among other things, the Austrian Netherlands.
15553.m: The Treaty of Campo Formio of 1797 crowned Napoleon's Italian campaign.

15554.q: Over which Alpine pass did Napoleon lead his reserve army into Italy in May 1800?
15554.e: In May 1800 Napoleon crossed the Great St Bernard between Valais and the Aosta Valley with his army. Shortly afterwards he won at Marengo on 14 June 1800.
15554.m: In 1800 Napoleon crossed the Great St Bernard into Italy.

15555.q: Which battle of 2 December 1805 is called the ‘Battle of the Three Emperors’?
15555.e: At Austerlitz in Moravia Napoleon defeated the armies of the Austrian and the Russian emperors. That is why it is called the Battle of the Three Emperors.
15555.m: Austerlitz in 1805 was one of Napoleon's greatest victories.

15556.q: Which British admiral defeated the French-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar on 21 October 1805 and was killed doing so?
15556.e: Admiral Nelson won the naval battle of Trafalgar but was fatally wounded. Great Britain thus secured control of the seas.
15556.m: Nelson's victory at Trafalgar secured Britain's rule of the seas.

15557.q: What was Napoleon's aim with the Continental System, which he imposed in Berlin on 21 November 1806?
a: To shut Russia out of trade
To close the Alpine passes to troops
15557.e: The Berlin Decree banned trade with Great Britain on the continent. Napoleon wanted to force the British to negotiate through an economic war.
15557.m: The Continental System was Napoleon's economic war against Great Britain.

15558.q: What is the connection between the Continental System and the Russian campaign of 1812?
a: Russia relaxed the blockade in 1810, which contributed to the conflict with Napoleon
Russia demanded a stricter blockade and attacked France
The blockade forced Great Britain to attack Russia
Napoleon lifted the blockade to win Russia over
15558.e: At the end of 1810 the Tsar again allowed trade in British goods under neutral flags. Russia thus effectively left the Continental System, which increased tensions until war broke out.
15558.m: The dispute over the Continental System was one cause of the Russian campaign.

15559.q: Which state was defeated in the double battle of Jena and Auerstedt on 14 October 1806?
15559.e: Prussia had declared war on France in October 1806 and lost at Jena and Auerstedt. The defeat later triggered major reforms in Prussia.
15559.m: Jena and Auerstedt in 1806 meant the collapse of the old Prussia.

15560.q: What was the union of German states founded in 1806 under Napoleon's protection called?
15560.e: In July 1806 southern and western German states joined the Confederation of the Rhine and broke away from the Empire. The German Confederation only came into being in 1815.
15560.m: In 1806 the Confederation of the Rhine tied many German states to Napoleon.

a: The Holy Roman Empire came to an end
The Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved
15561.e: Under pressure from Napoleon, Emperor Francis II laid down the imperial crown of the Holy Roman Empire. This ended the Empire after more than 800 years.
15561.m: The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806 under pressure from Napoleon.

15562.q: From which conflict does the term ‘guerrilla’ for small-scale warfare come?
a: From the Spanish resistance against Napoleon from 1808
From the American War of Independence
15562.e: From 1808 Spanish rebels fought against the French troops in small groups. The Spanish word for ‘little war’ became the term for this form of fighting.
15562.m: The term guerrilla comes from the Spanish resistance against Napoleon.

15563.q: Roughly how many soldiers in total marched into Russia with the Grande Armée in 1812, including reinforcements?
15563.e: On the night of 23 to 24 June 1812 the crossing of the Neman began, at first with around 450,000 men. With reinforcements there were around 600,000 soldiers from many countries in total, of whom only a small part returned.
15563.m: Napoleon's Grande Armée numbered around 600,000 men in 1812.

15564.q: Why is the Battle of the Berezina in November 1812 important for Swiss history?
a: Swiss regiments covered the retreat with heavy losses
Switzerland declared war on Russia there
Swiss troops fought for the Tsar
15564.e: Around 1,300 Swiss in Marshal Ney's corps held off the Russians while the army crossed the bridges. Only about 300 were still present at roll call afterwards.
15564.m: At the Berezina in 1812 Swiss regiments sacrificed themselves for the Grande Armée's retreat.

15565.q: Which song is linked in memory with the Swiss soldiers at the Berezina?
15565.e: An officer is said to have sung the song shortly before the fighting on 28 November 1812. Through eyewitness accounts it became known as the Beresinalied.
15565.m: The Beresinalied commemorates the Swiss in the Russian campaign.

15566.q: Which powers fought against Napoleon in the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig from 16 to 19 October 1813?
a: Great Britain, Spain, Portugal and Holland
Austria, Spain, Naples and Great Britain
15566.e: The allies Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden defeated Napoleon at Leipzig. With up to 600,000 men involved, it was one of the largest battles before the 20th century.
15566.m: The Battle of the Nations at Leipzig in 1813 broke Napoleon's rule in Germany.

15567.q: What is Napoleon's renewed rule, from his return from Elba in 1815 to his defeat at Waterloo, called?
15567.e: Napoleon left Elba at the end of February 1815, landed in France on 1 March and took power again. After Waterloo he finally abdicated on 22 June 1815.
15567.m: The Hundred Days were Napoleon's last attempt to win back power.

15568.q: Which commanders defeated Napoleon at Waterloo on 18 June 1815?
15568.e: The British general Wellington held out against the French army until the Prussians under Blücher joined in. Napoleon was thus finally defeated.
15568.m: Wellington and Blücher defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815.

15569.q: In which present-day country is the battlefield of Waterloo?
15569.e: Waterloo lies about 15 kilometres south of Brussels. At the time the area belonged to the United Kingdom of the Netherlands; today it is part of Belgium.
15569.m: The battlefield of Waterloo lies south of Brussels in Belgium.

15570.q: In which battle were the Bernese defeated by French troops on 5 March 1798?
15570.e: The Bernese were beaten at Grauholz, and Bern surrendered the same day. The Bernese did win at Neuenegg, but that did not change the outcome.
15570.m: With the fall of Bern in 1798 the Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed.

15571.q: When and where was the Helvetic Republic constituted?
15571.e: On 12 April 1798 the deputies met in Aarau and adopted the constitution. Aarau was the first, provisional capital.
15571.m: The Helvetic Republic began on 12 April 1798 in Aarau.

15572.q: Which Basel politician drafted the first Helvetic constitution on behalf of France?
15572.e: In January 1798 Peter Ochs presented his draft constitution, which closely followed the French model. This constitution is considered the first modern constitution on present-day Swiss territory.
15572.m: The first Helvetic constitution was written by Peter Ochs.

15573.q: Which principle of the state shaped the Helvetic Republic?
15573.e: The cantons became mere administrative districts without their own sovereignty. Power lay with the central government, on the French model.
15573.m: The Helvetic Republic tried to govern Switzerland as a unitary state.

15574.q: What was the five-member government of the Helvetic Republic, modelled on France, called?
15574.e: The Directory had five members and was modelled on the French Directory. It was abolished in a coup at the beginning of 1800.
15574.m: The Helvetic Republic was first governed by a five-member Directory.

15575.q: Which patriot from Vaud was tutor to the future Tsar Alexander I?
15575.e: La Harpe was a tutor at the Tsar's court and fought against Bernese rule over Vaud. He became a member of the Helvetic Directory.
15575.m: La Harpe worked to free Vaud from Bern.

15576.q: Which republic was proclaimed in Vaud on 24 January 1798?
15576.e: Vaud broke away from Bern and proclaimed the Lemanic Republic. Shortly afterwards it became part of the Helvetic Republic.
15576.m: With the Lemanic Republic Vaud freed itself from Bern in 1798.

15577.q: Which of these cantons existed only during the Helvetic Republic?
15577.e: On 2 May 1798 the cantons of Linth, Säntis and Waldstätten were created by merging old cantons. With the Act of Mediation they disappeared again.
15577.m: The cantons of Linth, Säntis and Waldstätten existed only in the Helvetic Republic.

15578.q: What happened in 1798 to former subject territories such as Thurgau, Lugano or Baden?
a: They became cantons with equal rights
15578.e: The Helvetic Republic abolished the subject relationships and turned the former bailiwicks into cantons. The inhabitants became Helvetic citizens with equal rights.
15578.m: The Helvetic Republic ended subject relationships in Switzerland.

15579.q: Which innovation did the Helvetic Republic bring in 1798?
a: Abolition of privileges, feudal dues and guild rights
Founding of the Swiss National Bank
Introduction of compulsory schooling for adults
15579.e: The Helvetic Republic placed equality before the law above old privileges, abolished personal feudal duties and the privileges of the guilds in 1798 and restricted tithes and ground rents. But this was only partly carried out, and some dues were later reintroduced.
15579.m: The Helvetic Republic put equality before the law above old privileges.

15580.q: Which part of the country experienced the so-called ‘days of terror’ in September 1798, when French troops crushed an uprising?
15580.e: Nidwalden refused to swear the oath to the Helvetic constitution. On 9 September 1798 French troops bloodily crushed the resistance.
15580.m: Nidwalden's resistance to the Helvetic Republic ended in bloodshed in 1798.

15581.q: Which educator looked after children orphaned by the war in Stans in 1799?
15581.e: After the fighting in Nidwalden, Pestalozzi ran an orphanage in Stans in 1799. His experiences there shaped his theory of education.
15581.m: In 1799 Pestalozzi cared for war orphans in Stans.

15582.q: What did the Helvetic Republic ask teachers all over the country about in a large survey in 1799?
a: About the state of their schools
About their political opinion of France
About war damage in their villages
15582.e: In 1799 Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer had teachers questioned about pupils, lessons and school buildings. The answers to this Stapfer survey give a unique insight into everyday school life around 1800.
15582.m: The Stapfer survey shows the state of schools around 1800.

15583.q: Which city was the scene of two battles between France and its enemies in 1799?
15583.e: In the War of the Second Coalition the French, Austrians and Russians fought on Swiss soil. There were battles near Zurich in June and in September 1799.
15583.m: In 1799 Switzerland became a battleground for foreign armies.

15584.q: Which Russian commander marched an army over the Gotthard and through central Switzerland in autumn 1799?
15584.e: Suvorov wanted to join up with the Russian troops near Zurich. After their defeat he had to retreat over the Alps with heavy losses.
15584.m: Suvorov's crossing of the Alps in 1799 is still remembered in central Switzerland.

15585.q: At which bridge in the Schöllenen gorge does a monument commemorate Suvorov's crossing of the Alps in 1799?
15585.e: In the Schöllenen Russian and French troops fought for the crossing at the Devil's Bridge. A monument carved into the rock commemorates the fallen Russians.
15585.m: The Suvorov monument stands by the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen.

15586.q: Where does the Stecklikrieg (‘War of the Sticks’) of 1802 get its name from?
a: From the clubs that many rebels were armed with
From the village of Stecklingen in Aargau
From the posts of the border fortifications
15586.e: Because they lacked rifles, many peasant rebels carried only sticks. The short civil war was directed against the Helvetic central government.
15586.m: The Stecklikrieg is named after the rebels' sticks.

15587.q: Where did Swiss deputies discuss a new order for Switzerland with Napoleon from December 1802?
15587.e: In the so-called Helvetic Consulta, deputies from both camps met in Paris from 10 December 1802. The result was the Act of Mediation.
15587.m: The Act of Mediation was negotiated in Paris in 1802 and 1803.

15588.q: In which year did Napoleon hand over the Act of Mediation to Switzerland?
15588.e: Napoleon handed over the Act of Mediation on 19 February 1803. It ended the Helvetic Republic and was the constitutional basis of Switzerland until the end of 1813.
15588.m: The Act of Mediation of 1803 ended the Helvetic Republic.

15589.q: Where does the name of the Mediation period come from?
a: Napoleon acted as mediator between the parties
Switzerland lay in the middle of Europe
The cantons mediated between France and Austria
A treaty was named after the town of Mediation
15589.e: Mediation means acting as a go-between. Napoleon mediated between Unitarians and Federalists and called himself Mediator of Switzerland.
15589.m: Mediation means acting as a go-between, and Napoleon was the mediator.

15590.q: How many cantons did Switzerland have under the Act of Mediation?
15590.e: The 13 old cantons were restored and six new ones were created. Together that made 19 cantons.
15590.m: Switzerland under the Mediation had 19 cantons.

15591.q: Which group contains only cantons that were created as new cantons in 1803?
15591.e: The new cantons of 1803 were St Gallen, the Grisons, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud. Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel only joined in 1815, Jura and Basel-Landschaft even later.
15591.m: The six new cantons of 1803 were mostly former subject territories or associates.

15592.q: Which former Further Austrian territory became part of the new canton of Aargau in 1803?
15592.e: Austria had ceded the Fricktal to France in the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801, and France handed it to the Helvetic Republic in 1802. With the Act of Mediation it became part of the canton of Aargau in 1803.
15592.m: The Fricktal has belonged to the canton of Aargau since 1803.

15593.q: Which present-day canton was formed in 1803 from the former bailiwicks south of the Gotthard?
15593.e: In the Helvetic Republic the former subject territories south of the Gotthard formed the cantons of Lugano and Bellinzona. In 1803 they were united as the canton of Ticino.
15593.m: The canton of Ticino was formed in 1803 from former subject territories.

15594.q: Which territories did Bern finally lose with the Act of Mediation of 1803?
a: The Bernese Oberland and the Emmental
15594.e: The former Bernese subject territories of Vaud and Aargau became independent cantons. Even so, Bern remained one of the largest cantons.
15594.m: Since 1803 Vaud and Aargau have been separate cantons.

15595.q: What was the highest office in Switzerland during the Mediation period, which changed every year, called?
15595.e: The Landammann of Switzerland was always the head of the canton that served as the leading canton for one year. The first Landammann in 1803 was Louis d'Affry of Fribourg.
15595.m: In the Mediation period a Landammann who changed every year led Switzerland.

15596.q: What was the ‘Vorort’ (leading canton) in the Mediation period?
a: The canton that led the Confederacy for one year at a time
The main town of each canton
A French military base in Switzerland
15596.e: Six directorial cantons took turns each year as the leading canton: Fribourg, Bern, Solothurn, Basel, Zurich and Lucerne. Their chief magistrate or mayor was then Landammann of Switzerland.
15596.m: In the Mediation period the leading canton ran Switzerland for one year at a time.

15597.q: What form of state did Switzerland have after the Act of Mediation?
a: A confederation of largely independent cantons
A federal state with a Federal Council
15597.e: The Act of Mediation gave up the unitary state and largely gave the cantons back their sovereignty. Their common body was the Diet.
15597.m: The Act of Mediation made Switzerland a confederation of states again.

15598.q: What did Switzerland commit to in the military alliance with France of September 1803?
a: To close the Alpine passes for France
To supply France with gold every year
15598.e: In peacetime France was allowed to recruit 16,000 men in Switzerland. The cantons often struggled to provide the troops demanded.
15598.m: In the Mediation period Switzerland had to supply Napoleon with soldiers.

15599.q: What is the uprising of 1804 in municipalities on Lake Zurich called?
15599.e: In spring 1804 municipalities on Lake Zurich rose up. The Diet had the uprising crushed and the leaders executed.
15599.m: The Bockenkrieg of 1804 was an uprising on Lake Zurich.

15600.q: What was the Bockenkrieg of 1804 mainly directed against?
a: The laws on buying off tithes and ground rents
15600.e: The rural population felt that the conditions for buying off the old feudal dues were unfair. They felt cheated of what the Helvetic Republic had achieved.
15600.m: The Bockenkrieg was about buying off the old feudal dues.

a: It was annexed to France as the département of Simplon
It went to the Kingdom of Sardinia
15601.e: Valais had been a separate republic since 1802. In 1810 Napoleon incorporated it into France as the département of Simplon in order to control the Simplon Pass.

15602.q: Which power did the Principality of Neuchâtel belong to before 1806 and again from 1814?
15602.e: From 1707 Neuchâtel was owned by the King of Prussia. In 1806 Prussia ceded it to Napoleon, who installed his marshal Berthier as prince. From 1814 it was Prussian again and, from 1815, also a Swiss canton.
15602.m: For a long time Neuchâtel was a principality of the King of Prussia.

15603.q: Which event at the end of December 1813 began the end of the Mediation period?
a: Switzerland joined the Confederation of the Rhine
15603.e: On 21 December 1813 allied troops crossed the Swiss border. A few days later several cantons abolished the Mediation constitution.
15603.m: With Napoleon's decline the Mediation period also ended at the end of 1813.

15604.q: From when to when did the Congress of Vienna last?
15604.e: The congress began on 18 September 1814. The Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, a few days before Waterloo.
15604.m: The Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe in 1814 and 1815.

15605.q: Who represented defeated France at the Congress of Vienna?
15605.e: Talleyrand negotiated for the France of the restored King Louis XVIII. He skilfully made sure that France could again have its say as a great power.
15605.m: Talleyrand successfully represented France at the Congress of Vienna.

15606.q: What did the principle of legitimacy mean at the Congress of Vienna?
a: The rightful old dynasties should rule again
All peoples should have their own states
Rulers should be elected by the people
The Church should choose the princes
15606.e: The ruling houses removed by Napoleon were to return to their thrones. For example, the Bourbons returned in France.
15606.m: Legitimacy meant the return of the traditional ruling houses.

15607.q: What was meant by the Restoration after the Congress of Vienna?
a: The return to pre-revolutionary political conditions
The introduction of constitutions in all states
The return of stolen works of art
15607.e: The princes wanted to restore the order before the Revolution as far as possible. Liberal and national movements were to be suppressed.
15607.m: The Restoration wanted to bring back the order before 1789.

15608.q: What was the aim of the principle of the balance of power?
a: No great power should be able to dominate Europe
All states should become the same size
All rulers should receive the same amount of money
Borders should be drawn along language lines
15608.e: After the experience with Napoleon, no state was to become too powerful. A balanced distribution of power was meant to prevent major wars.
15608.m: The balance of power was meant to prevent wars after 1815.

15609.q: What does the saying ‘The Congress dances’ about the Congress of Vienna refer to?
a: To the many balls and parties while the negotiations hardly moved forward
To a new dance invented in Vienna
To the quick agreement of all the powers
To a dispute settled by a dance competition
15609.e: In 1814 the Prince de Ligne wrote, in effect, that the Congress danced but did not make progress. Vienna offered the diplomats many balls and parties.
15609.m: The saying about the dancing Congress criticised the slow negotiations.

15610.q: Which event disrupted the ongoing negotiations in Vienna in March 1815?
a: The death of Tsar Alexander I
The eruption of the volcano Tambora
15610.e: Napoleon landed in France on 1 March 1815. The powers renewed their alliance and speeded up the negotiations.
15610.m: Napoleon's return in 1815 brought the Congress powers back together.

15611.q: Which confederation of states was created in 1815 by the German Federal Act?
15611.e: The German Federal Act was signed on 8 June 1815. The German Confederation was a loose union of sovereign states with Austria as the presiding power.
15611.m: In 1815 the German Confederation replaced the old Empire as a loose confederation of states.

15612.q: Which power received most of Poland at the Congress of Vienna as so-called Congress Poland?
15612.e: The Kingdom of Poland was joined to Russia in a personal union. Kraków became a small, guaranteed republic.
15612.m: After 1815 Congress Poland was under Russian rule.

15613.q: Which territories in the west did Prussia gain at the Congress of Vienna?
15613.e: Prussia received, among other things, the Rhineland, Westphalia and part of Saxony. This brought it up to the border with France.
15613.m: With the Rhineland and Westphalia Prussia became a power on the Rhine in 1815.

15614.q: Which states formed the Holy Alliance on 26 September 1815?
15614.e: The three monarchs promised each other to rule according to Christian principles and to support one another. The alliance served mainly to fight off revolutionary movements.
15614.m: In 1815 the Holy Alliance united the three conservative eastern powers.

15615.q: Which three territories were recognised as new Swiss cantons at the Congress of Vienna?
15615.e: The three territories were admitted to the Confederacy in 1814 and 1815 and anchored as cantons in the Federal Treaty. The Congress of Vienna confirmed this enlargement.
15615.m: Since 1815 Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva have belonged to the Confederacy.

15616.q: Which canton received most of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel as compensation at the Congress of Vienna?
15616.e: Bern received the area of today's Jura and the Bernese Jura in place of the lost Vaud and Aargau. This later gave rise to the Jura question.
15616.m: In 1815 the Jura went to Bern as compensation.

15617.q: Which former subject territories of the Grisons did Switzerland not get back in 1815?
15617.e: The territories had been lost to the Cisalpine Republic in 1797. In 1815 they went to Austria, and today they belong to Italy.
15617.m: After 1815 Valtellina remained separated from the Grisons.

15618.q: Which new state was created at the Congress of Vienna from the northern and southern Netherlands?
15618.e: The Austrian Netherlands were united with the northern Netherlands. This state was meant to contain France in the north; Belgium broke away from it in 1830.
15618.m: The United Kingdom of the Netherlands was a bulwark against France.

15619.q: On the day of which peace treaty, 20 November 1815, did the great powers in Paris recognise Switzerland's perpetual neutrality?
15619.e: On the same day as the Second Treaty of Paris, the signatory powers signed a declaration in Paris that recognised and guaranteed Switzerland's perpetual neutrality. In terms of the balance of power, it was in Europe's interest.
15619.m: Switzerland's perpetual neutrality was recognised on 20 November 1815.

15620.q: Which Geneva diplomat worked especially hard for the recognition of Swiss neutrality in 1814 and 1815?
15620.e: Pictet de Rochemont represented Geneva and Switzerland at the negotiations in Vienna and Paris. He is seen as the main champion of a neutral Switzerland.
15620.m: Pictet de Rochemont was Switzerland's most important diplomat in 1815.

15621.q: Besides neutrality, what did the great powers expressly guarantee in 1815?
15621.e: The declaration of 1815 guaranteed neutrality and the inviolability of the territory within the borders of 1815. Switzerland in turn committed itself to remaining neutral in future conflicts.
15621.m: Neutrality and the inviolability of the territory were guaranteed together in 1815.

15622.q: What does the term ‘perpetual neutrality’ mean?
a: A state stays neutral in all future wars
A state stays neutral only in the current war
A state may never have an army
A state may not make any treaties
15622.e: With perpetual or permanent neutrality a state commits itself for all time not to take part in wars. Occasional neutrality, on the other hand, applies only to a particular conflict.
15622.m: Perpetual neutrality applies permanently, not just for one war.

15623.q: To which neighbouring area was Swiss neutrality extended in 1815?
15623.e: The neutralisation included parts of Savoy, which then belonged to Sardinia-Piedmont. In case of war Switzerland would have been allowed to occupy this area.
15623.m: The neutrality of 1815 included parts of Savoy.

15624.q: Which battle was long seen as the start of the Swiss tradition of neutrality, a view that is now strongly qualified?
15624.e: After the defeat at Marignano the Confederates gave up their own great-power politics. More recent research, however, does not yet see this as neutrality in the modern sense.
15624.m: Modern Swiss neutrality only begins in international law in 1815.

15625.q: What did the march of allied troops through Switzerland at the end of 1813 show?
a: That merely declared neutrality without recognition was not respected
That Switzerland was allied with the allies
15625.e: The Diet had declared neutrality in 1813, but the allies marched through the country anyway. Only in 1815 was neutrality recognised in international law.
15625.m: Without recognition by the great powers, Swiss neutrality had no effect in 1813.

15626.q: Why was a neutral Switzerland in the interest of the great powers in 1815?
a: As a buffer state with important Alpine passes it separated France and Austria
It supplied mercenaries to all great powers
It was the strongest military power in Europe
15626.e: A neutral Switzerland prevented any one power from controlling the Alpine passes and the area between France and Austria. This fitted the balance-of-power thinking of the Congress of Vienna.
15626.m: In 1815 Swiss neutrality also served the balance of power.

15627.q: Which duty follows for Switzerland from the principle of armed neutrality?
a: It must be able to defend its territory itself
It must supply troops to all warring parties
It must let foreign armies march through
15627.e: A neutral state may not hand over its territory to foreign armies. That is why Switzerland keeps its own army for national defence.
15627.m: Armed neutrality means protecting your own territory yourself.

15628.q: Which agreement first set out the law of neutrality comprehensively in 1907?
15628.e: The Hague Conventions of 1907 laid down the rights and duties of neutral states in war. The basis of Swiss neutrality, however, remained the recognition of 1815.
15628.m: The Hague Convention of 1907 codified the law of neutrality.

15629.q: How did Switzerland behave during Napoleon's Hundred Days in 1815?
a: It took the side of the allies
It stayed completely uninvolved, without an army
15629.e: In 1815 Switzerland joined the allies, let troops through and even advanced briefly into Franche-Comté. Full neutrality was only recognised afterwards.
15629.m: In 1815 Switzerland was on the allies' side against Napoleon.

15630.q: Which document formed the basis of the Confederacy from 1815 to 1848?
15630.e: The Federal Treaty was agreed in 1814 and came into force on 7 August 1815. It made Switzerland a loose confederation of states again.
15630.m: The Federal Treaty of 1815 applied until the Federal Constitution of 1848.

15631.q: What is the Diet that discussed the reorganisation of Switzerland from April 1814 to August 1815 called?
15631.e: The Long Diet met in Zurich from 6 April 1814 to 31 August 1815. It drew up the Federal Treaty.
15631.m: The Long Diet created the Federal Treaty in 1814 and 1815.

15632.q: Which cantons took turns as leading canton under the Federal Treaty of 1815?
15632.e: Under the Federal Treaty the leadership of the Diet changed every two years between Zurich, Bern and Lucerne. There was no fixed capital.
15632.m: After 1815 Zurich, Bern and Lucerne took turns as leading canton.

15633.q: When did Geneva become part of the Confederacy?
a: In 1815, after the end of Napoleonic rule
15633.e: The Diet decided to admit Geneva in September 1814, and the treaty of union followed in May 1815. Geneva thus became the 22nd canton.
15633.m: Geneva became the 22nd canton of Switzerland in 1815.

15634.q: Why is the Final Act of the Congress of Vienna an important source for Switzerland?
a: It records Switzerland's new borders and cantons
It contains the first Federal Constitution
15634.e: The Final Act of 9 June 1815 confirmed, among other things, Switzerland's cantons and territorial changes such as the Jura going to Bern. Switzerland's borders were thus fixed in international law.
15634.m: The Final Act of Vienna fixed Switzerland's borders in 1815.

15635.q: Which period in Swiss history is called the Restoration?
15635.e: After the end of the Mediation period in 1813/14, the old elites tried to restore the conditions before the Revolution. The era ended when liberal reforms began in many cantons in 1830.
15635.m: In Switzerland the Restoration lasted from 1814 to 1830.

15636.q: Which treaty regulated relations between the cantons from 1815?
15636.e: The Federal Treaty was sworn on 7 August 1815 in Zurich’s Grossmünster. It made Switzerland a loose confederation of states again.
15636.m: The Federal Treaty of 1815 created a loose confederation of states again.

15637.q: How many cantons swore the Federal Treaty of 1815?
15637.e: With three new cantons admitted, the number rose to 22. This number stayed the same until the canton of Jura was founded in 1979.
15637.m: From 1815 the Confederation consisted of 22 cantons.

15638.q: Which three territories joined the Confederation as new cantons in 1815?
a: The Grisons, St Gallen and Thurgau
15638.e: The Congress of Vienna recognised the enlargement of the Confederation in the west. With this, Switzerland essentially got its present borders.
15638.m: Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel became Swiss cantons in 1815.

15639.q: What was special about the canton of Neuchâtel after 1815?
a: It was also a principality of the King of Prussia.
It had no vote in the Federal Diet.
It was a subject territory of Bern.
