15639.e: Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time a principality owned by the Prussian king. This double status later led to a serious conflict with Prussia.
15639.m: After 1815 Neuchâtel was both a canton and a Prussian principality.

15640.q: Which cities took turns as the leading canton (Vorort) after the Federal Treaty of 1815?
15640.e: The Vorort ran the business of the Federal Diet and changed every two years. However, it had no special privileges.
15640.m: Zurich, Bern and Lucerne took turns as the Vorort of the Confederation.

15641.q: When did the great powers formally recognise Switzerland’s perpetual neutrality?
15641.e: The declaration of 20 November 1815 was connected with the Second Peace of Paris. The Congress of Vienna had already promised recognition in March 1815.
15641.m: Swiss neutrality was recognised by the great powers in 1815.

15642.q: What did the old elites in Switzerland want to achieve during the Restoration from 1814?
a: To restore conditions as they were before the French Revolution
To found a modern federal state
15642.e: Restoration means bringing back. After Napoleon’s fall, the old rulers wanted to win back their privileges from before 1798.
15642.m: The Restoration tried to bring back the old order from before 1798.

15643.q: Under whose pressure did the Federal Diet restrict press freedom and asylum for political refugees in 1823?
a: Under pressure from great powers such as Austria and Prussia
15643.e: The conservative great powers wanted to stop liberal refugees from spreading propaganda from Switzerland. The Federal Diet therefore decided on stricter rules in 1823.
15643.m: Under pressure from the great powers, Switzerland restricted the press and asylum in 1823.

15644.q: What caused the famine years of 1816 and 1817 in Switzerland?
a: The eruption of the Tambora volcano and failed harvests
A cattle plague on the Central Plateau
15644.e: The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia led to the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816. The failed harvests caused the last great famine in Swiss history.
15644.m: A volcanic eruption caused the famine of 1816 and 1817.

15645.q: Which alliance of monarchs did Switzerland join in 1817?
15645.e: The Holy Alliance of Russia, Austria and Prussia was meant to secure the monarchical order. Switzerland joining in 1817 shows the conservative direction of the Restoration period.
15645.m: Switzerland joined the Holy Alliance in 1817.

15646.q: How did the old elites in cities such as Bern secure their power during the Restoration?
a: By restoring the patriciate and voting rights based on wealth
15646.e: In Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn the old patrician families ruled again. Voting rights based on wealth and indirect elections kept most citizens away from power.
15646.m: The patriciate and wealth-based voting rights secured power for the old elites.

15647.q: Which event abroad triggered the Regeneration in many cantons in 1830?
15647.e: The July Revolution in Paris encouraged the liberals in Switzerland. In 1830 and 1831 many cantons got new, liberal constitutions.
15647.m: The July Revolution of 1830 set off the Regeneration in Switzerland.

15648.q: What is meant by the Regeneration in Swiss history?
a: The liberal renewal of many cantonal constitutions from 1830
The rebuilding after the Sonderbund War
The return to the old order after 1815
The reforestation of the woods in the 19th century
15648.e: From 1830 many cantons gave themselves new, liberal constitutions with popular sovereignty and civil liberties. This period is called the Regeneration, meaning renewal.
15648.m: The Regeneration from 1830 brought liberal cantonal constitutions.

15649.q: What was the Ustertag of 22 November 1830?
a: A popular assembly of the Zurich countryside calling for a new constitution
A battle between Zurich and Schwyz
The first sitting of the National Council
An uprising against the Federal Constitution
15649.e: In Uster the rural population demanded more political say and fairer representation in the Grand Council. The Ustertag led to the liberal Zurich constitution of 1831.
15649.m: At the Ustertag in 1830 the Zurich countryside demanded more rights.

15650.q: Which freedom did the liberals of the Regeneration demand most, so they could spread their ideas in newspapers?
15650.e: For the liberals, newspapers were the most important way to promote their ideas. The regenerated constitutions therefore guaranteed freedom of the press.
15650.m: The liberals of the Regeneration fought for freedom of the press.

15651.q: Which principle did the regenerated cantonal constitutions establish against the old order?
15651.e: The new constitutions declared the people to be the source of state power. They also guaranteed equality before the law, separation of powers and civil liberties such as freedom of the press.
15651.m: The Regeneration made the people the source of state power.

15652.q: Which canton was split in 1833 after fierce conflicts between town and countryside?
15652.e: After fighting between the city and the countryside, the division into Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft was finally recognised in 1833. Basel-Landschaft had already set itself up as a canton of its own in 1832.
15652.m: Basel was split into two half-cantons in 1833.

15653.q: Which liberal cantons joined together in the Concordat of Seven in 1832?
a: Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn, St Gallen, Aargau and Thurgau
Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug, Lucerne and Valais
Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and Bern
Basel, Schaffhausen, Glarus, Appenzell, the Grisons, Zug and Uri
15653.e: The seven cantons guaranteed each other’s new liberal constitutions. In this way they wanted to protect themselves against conservative coups.
15653.m: In the Concordat of Seven, seven liberal cantons protected their constitutions.

15654.q: What was the alliance of conservative cantons formed in response to the Concordat of Seven called?
15654.e: In November 1832 Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt, among others, joined together in the League of Sarnen. It rejected the liberal innovations.
15654.m: The League of Sarnen was the conservative counter-alliance of 1832.

15655.q: What did the Rossi Plan of 1832/33 aim to achieve?
a: A reform of the loose Federal Treaty of 1815
The division of the canton of Basel
The restoration of the Helvetic Republic
15655.e: Pellegrino Rossi’s draft wanted to bring the Confederation more closely together. It did not go far enough for the radicals and went too far for the conservatives, and it failed in the cantons in 1833.
15655.m: The Rossi Plan aimed to reform the Federal Treaty and failed in 1833.

15656.q: Which university was founded in 1833 in the spirit of the Regeneration?
15656.e: Liberal governments promoted education as the basis of responsible citizens. Zurich founded its university in 1833, and Bern followed in 1834.
15656.m: The University of Zurich was founded in 1833 during the Regeneration.

15657.q: What led to the Züriputsch in 1839?
a: The appointment of the theologian David Friedrich Strauss
The introduction of new taxes on wine
The building of the first railway
The closing of the monasteries in Aargau
15657.e: The appointment of the controversial theologian as professor outraged the conservative rural population. On 6 September 1839 an uprising overthrew the liberal government.
15657.m: The dispute over David Friedrich Strauss led to the Züriputsch in 1839.

15658.q: Which word, now also used in English, spread through the whole German-speaking world because of the Zurich coup of 1839?
15658.e: The Swiss German word for a violent push became known through the reports on the Züriputsch. Today it generally means a violent overthrow of a government.
15658.m: The word “putsch” comes from Swiss German.

15659.e: The Catholic conservative cantons formed a defensive alliance at the end of 1845. The liberal majority saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty.
15659.m: The Sonderbund was founded in December 1845.

15660.q: Which canton did NOT belong to the Sonderbund?
15660.e: The members were Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Catholic Solothurn, like Appenzell Innerrhoden, stayed out of the alliance.
15660.m: Solothurn did not join the Sonderbund despite its Catholic majority.

15661.q: Which city was the centre of the Sonderbund?
15661.e: The Sonderbund was founded in Lucerne, and its war council sat there. Lucerne was also the member canton with the largest population.
15661.m: Lucerne was the political centre of the Sonderbund.

15662.q: Who chaired the war council of the Sonderbund?
15662.e: The Lucerne government councillor Constantin Siegwart-Müller was the leading figure of the Sonderbund. After the defeat he fled abroad.
15662.m: Constantin Siegwart-Müller led the war council of the Sonderbund.

15663.q: What happened in the Aargau monastery dispute of 1841?
a: The canton of Aargau closed the monasteries.
The Pope banned all Swiss monasteries.
The Federal Diet founded new monasteries.
15663.e: In January 1841 Aargau decided to close all its monasteries, which broke the Federal Treaty. The dispute poisoned relations between liberals and Catholic conservatives.
15663.m: The closing of the Aargau monasteries in 1841 sharpened the religious dispute.

15664.q: Which decision by the canton of Lucerne in 1844 particularly outraged the liberals?
a: Bringing the Jesuits in to run the higher school
15664.e: For the radicals, the Jesuits were a symbol of Rome and backwardness. Their appointment in Lucerne in 1844 triggered the Freischarenzüge.
15664.m: Bringing the Jesuits to Lucerne in 1844 fuelled the conflict.

15665.q: What were the Freischarenzüge of 1844 and 1845?
a: Armed attacks on Lucerne by radical volunteers
Campaigns by the Federal Diet against Valais
15665.e: Radical volunteers tried to overthrow the conservative government of Lucerne. Both expeditions failed, the second on 31 March 1845 with many taken prisoner.
15665.m: The volunteer expeditions against Lucerne failed in 1844 and 1845.

15666.q: Which later member of the first Federal Council led the second volunteer expedition in 1845?
15666.e: Ulrich Ochsenbein from Bern led the failed expedition against Lucerne. In 1848 he was elected to the first Federal Council.
15666.m: Ulrich Ochsenbein led the second volunteer expedition.

15667.q: Why did the liberal majority consider the Sonderbund illegal?
a: The Federal Treaty banned alliances that harmed the Confederation or other cantons.
It had been founded by France.
It had introduced its own currency.
It consisted only of Protestant cantons.
15667.e: The Federal Treaty of 1815 forbade the cantons from forming harmful separate alliances. The Federal Diet therefore declared the Sonderbund dissolved in 1847.
15667.m: In the majority’s view the Sonderbund broke the Federal Treaty.

15668.q: Which change in Geneva and St Gallen gave the liberals a majority in the Federal Diet in 1847?
a: Both cantons were occupied by Austria.
15668.e: Through the change of power in Geneva and the liberal election victory in St Gallen, the liberals reached the majority they needed. Only then could the Federal Diet decide to dissolve the Sonderbund.
15668.m: Only the turnaround in Geneva and St Gallen gave the liberals their majority in 1847.

15669.q: From which great power did the Sonderbund mainly hope for military help?
15669.e: The Sonderbund cantons negotiated in Vienna, Paris and Turin. Austria supplied some money and weapons but sent no troops.
15669.m: The Sonderbund hoped in vain for help from Austria.

15670.q: Who led the federal troops as general in the Sonderbund War of 1847?
15670.e: Dufour from Geneva ended the war in less than four weeks with few casualties. He ordered his troops to treat the wounded and prisoners well.
15670.m: General Dufour led the Federal Diet’s troops in 1847.

15671.q: Who was commander-in-chief of the federal troops in the Sonderbund War?
15671.e: The Federal Diet elected Dufour from Geneva as general. He led a quick campaign and tried to keep losses low.
15671.m: General Dufour led the federal army in the Sonderbund War.

15672.q: Roughly how long did the Sonderbund War last?
15672.e: The fighting began on 3 November 1847 and ended on 29 November with the surrender of Valais. So the war lasted only 26 days.
15672.m: The Sonderbund War lasted less than a month.

15673.q: Which Sonderbund canton was the last to surrender?
15673.e: On 29 November 1847 Valais surrendered as the last canton. With that, the war was over.
15673.m: The Sonderbund War ended with the surrender of Valais.

15674.q: Which battle on 23 November 1847 decided the fight for Lucerne?
15674.e: At Gisikon on the river Reuss the federal troops prevailed. The next day the city of Lucerne surrendered.
15674.m: The battle at Gisikon decided the fight for Lucerne.

15675.q: What was the Sonderbund that was defeated in the war of 1847?
a: A defensive alliance of Catholic conservative cantons
An alliance of the liberal cities
15675.e: Seven Catholic conservative cantons joined together in 1845 to form the Sonderbund. The liberal majority of the Federal Diet declared the alliance incompatible with the Federal Treaty.
15675.m: The Sonderbund was an alliance of Catholic conservative cantons.

15676.q: With which attack did the Sonderbund War begin on 3 November 1847?
a: With an advance by Sonderbund troops into Ticino
15676.e: Sonderbund troops advanced over the Gotthard into Ticino. On 4 November the Federal Diet decided to enforce its decision by force of arms.
15676.m: The war began with a Sonderbund advance into Ticino.

15677.q: How is the number of dead in the Sonderbund War usually estimated?
15677.e: Recent research gives just over 90 dead, official figures about 150. Compared with other civil wars, the losses remained low.
15677.m: The Sonderbund War caused relatively few deaths.

15678.q: Why is Dufour’s conduct of the war considered especially moderate?
a: He ordered that the wounded and prisoners be treated humanely.
He had the Sonderbund cantons occupied and looted.
He left the fighting to foreign mercenaries.
15678.e: Dufour did not want to humiliate his opponents, because they were to be fellow Confederates again after the war. He spared civilians and demanded good treatment of the wounded.
15678.m: Dufour fought the war with the later peace in mind.

15679.q: In which later founding did General Dufour play an important role?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
15679.e: In 1863 Dufour was part of the founding committee in Geneva from which the ICRC emerged. The highest Swiss summit, the Dufourspitze, is also named after him.
15679.m: General Dufour was one of the founders of the Red Cross.

15680.q: What important consequence did the quick victory in the Sonderbund War have?
a: The way was clear for the Federal Constitution of 1848.
The Jesuits became the state church.
The Federal Diet was strengthened and remained.
15680.e: After the liberals’ victory, the Federal Diet was able to revise the Federal Treaty completely. Because the great powers did not intervene, the federal state was created in 1848.
15680.m: Victory in the Sonderbund War made the Federal Constitution of 1848 possible.

15681.q: Why did the conservative great powers not intervene in the Sonderbund War in 1847?
a: The war was over too quickly and they had problems at home.
Switzerland was a member of NATO at the time.
An alliance with Great Britain forbade it.
15681.e: Austria and Prussia hesitated, and in 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe. The short war created a fait accompli before any intervention was possible.
15681.m: The shortness of the war prevented foreign interference.

15682.q: What date does Switzerland’s first Federal Constitution bear?
15682.e: The Federal Diet declared the constitution adopted on 12 September 1848. With that, the confederation of states became a federal state.
15682.m: The first Federal Constitution is dated 12 September 1848.

15683.q: Which model did the two-chamber system of the 1848 Federal Constitution follow?
a: The Reichstag of the German Empire
15683.e: The National Council and the Council of States correspond to the House of Representatives and the Senate of the USA. In this way the interests of the people and the cantons were taken into account equally.
15683.m: Switzerland’s two-chamber system follows the American model.

15684.q: Which compromise was the basis of the two-chamber system of 1848?
a: A balance between large and small cantons
A balance between the nobility and the middle class
A balance between church and state
A balance between the city of Bern and the city of Zurich
15684.e: In the National Council, cantons with large populations have more seats; in the Council of States, all cantons have the same number of seats. This made the small, defeated cantons more likely to accept the federal state.
15684.m: The two-chamber system combines representation of the people and of the cantons.

15685.q: Which cantons mostly rejected the Federal Constitution of 1848?
15685.e: A clear majority of men voted in favour. The constitution was rejected mainly by Catholic cantons such as Uri, Schwyz or Valais, which had been defeated in the Sonderbund War in 1847.
15685.m: In 1848 the constitution was rejected mainly by the losers of the Sonderbund War.

15686.q: How was the Federal Constitution decided on in the canton of Fribourg in 1848?
a: By the cantonal parliament instead of a popular vote
By the Bishop of Lausanne and Geneva
15686.e: The radical Fribourg government let the parliament decide in order to avoid rejection by the people. This shows that the votes of 1848 were not equally democratic everywhere.
15686.m: In Fribourg in 1848 the cantonal parliament decided on the constitution.

15687.q: Which responsibility passed from the cantons to the federal government in 1848?
15687.e: Internal customs duties between the cantons were dropped, and the federal government collected the border duties. This created a single economic area.
15687.m: Since 1848 customs have been a federal matter.

15688.q: Which areas were also standardised with the new federal state?
a: Post, coins, and weights and measures
Police, street names and public holidays
15688.e: Before that, almost every canton had its own coins and measures. Standardisation made trade and transport much easier.
15688.m: The federal state standardised post, money, and weights and measures.

15689.q: To whom did the freedom of establishment in the 1848 Federal Constitution at first apply?
a: Only to Swiss citizens of Christian denomination
Only to citizens of the towns
15689.e: Jews were excluded from the freedom of establishment. Only the partial revision of 1866 gave them equal rights on this point.
15689.m: In 1848 freedom of establishment applied only to Christian Swiss citizens.

15690.q: Which religious order was banned in Switzerland by the Federal Constitution of 1848?
15690.e: The ban on the Jesuits was a direct result of the Sonderbund conflict. It was only lifted in a popular vote in 1973.
15690.m: The Federal Constitution of 1848 banned the Jesuit order.

15691.q: Who was allowed to vote and stand for election in federal matters in 1848?
a: Men and women aged 21 and over
15691.e: The constitution introduced voting rights for men without any wealth requirement. However, the cantons often excluded people receiving poor relief, for example, and women only got the vote in 1971.
15691.m: In 1848 Swiss men got the right to vote and stand for election.

15692.q: Which popular right was already contained in the Federal Constitution of 1848?
a: The popular initiative for partial revision
15692.e: Every change to the Federal Constitution had to be put to the people and the cantons. In addition, 50,000 voters could demand a total revision.
15692.m: Since 1848 the people and the cantons have decided on changes to the constitution.

15693.q: How was the Federal Constitution of 1848 prepared?
a: By a revision committee of the Federal Diet
By a constitutional council elected by the people
By envoys of the great powers
15693.e: The Federal Diet set up a committee on 16 August 1847, which met from February 1848. It presented a draft in April 1848.
15693.m: A committee of the Federal Diet drew up the constitution of 1848.

15694.q: Who elected the members of the first Federal Council in November 1848?
a: The people at the ballot box
15694.e: The National Council and the Council of States met for the first time in November 1848 and together elected the seven Federal Councillors. To this day the United Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.
15694.m: The Federal Assembly has elected the Federal Council since 1848.

15695.q: Which politician from Ticino belonged to the first Federal Council of 1848?
15695.e: Stefano Franscini represented Italian-speaking Switzerland in the first Federal Council. He especially promoted statistics and education.
15695.m: Stefano Franscini was the first Federal Councillor from Ticino.

15696.q: What is Bern officially called, since Switzerland legally has no capital?
15696.e: In November 1848 the Federal Assembly chose Bern as the seat of the federal authorities. But the constitution says nothing about a capital, so Bern is called the federal city (Bundesstadt).
15696.m: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland.

15697.q: Which cities were Bern’s main rivals in the choice of the federal seat in 1848?
15697.e: Zurich was already the economic centre and was not to gain even more weight. Lucerne was politically weakened as the centre of the Sonderbund.
15697.m: Zurich and Lucerne lost out to Bern in the choice of the federal city.

15698.q: Which institution did Zurich get to make up for not becoming the federal city?
15698.e: ETH (then the Federal Polytechnic) opened in Zurich in 1855. It became the first federal university.

15699.q: When was the present Federal Palace in Bern inaugurated?
15699.e: The parliament building with the large dome opened in 1902. Before that, parliament met in other buildings in Bern.
15699.m: The Federal Palace in Bern was inaugurated in 1902.

15700.q: Which businessman and politician shaped railway building and the Gotthard Tunnel in the young federal state?
15700.e: Alfred Escher founded the Swiss Credit Institute (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt) and pushed forward the Gotthard Railway. He is considered one of the most influential business leaders of the 19th century.
15700.m: Alfred Escher was a pioneer of Swiss railway building.

15701.q: Who built most of the railway lines in Switzerland after the first Railway Act of 1852?
15701.e: The Act left railway building to the cantons and private companies. Only after the popular vote of 1898 were the large private railways nationalised.
15701.m: In the young federal state, private companies built the railways.

15702.q: Which party provided all the members of the Federal Council from 1848 to 1891?
a: The Free Democrats, also called Liberal Radicals
15702.e: The winners of the Sonderbund War governed alone for over four decades. Only in 1891 did the Catholic Conservatives get a seat.
15702.m: Until 1891 only Free Democrats sat in the Federal Council.

15703.q: Which political group got a seat on the Federal Council for the first time in 1891?
15703.e: After more than forty years of sole rule by the Free Democrats, Josef Zemp from Lucerne was elected in 1891. In this way the losers of the Sonderbund War were brought into government.
15703.m: In 1891 the Catholic Conservatives entered the Federal Council.

15704.q: Which conflict with Prussia was resolved in 1856/57 when the king gave up his rights?
15704.e: In 1856 royalists in Neuchâtel attempted a coup in favour of the Prussian king. After mediation, the king gave up his claims in 1857.
15704.m: With the Neuchâtel affair, Neuchâtel broke away from Prussia completely.

15705.q: What does it mean that the Federal Constitution was “totally revised” in 1874?
a: It was rewritten as a whole
Only a single article was changed
It only applied to some cantons
15705.e: In a total revision the whole constitution is revised and adopted again. In a partial revision only individual articles are changed. Switzerland had total revisions in 1874 and 1999.
15705.m: A total revision renews the whole constitution.

15706.q: What happened to the first draft of a total revision in 1872?
a: It was rejected by the people and the cantons.
It was introduced without a vote.
It was blocked by the army.
It only came into force in French-speaking Switzerland.
15706.e: The centralist draft was narrowly rejected by the people and clearly by the cantons on 12 May 1872. French-speaking Swiss and Catholics in particular feared too much centralisation.
15706.m: The overly centralist draft of 1872 was rejected.

15707.q: Which new popular right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 bring?
a: Election of the Federal Council by the people
15707.e: A referendum could now be called against federal laws. At first this needed 30,000 signatures.
15707.m: Since 1874 the people have been able to vote on federal laws.

15708.q: Where did the permanent Federal Supreme Court get its seat after 1874?
15708.e: The Federal Supreme Court became a permanent court based in Lausanne. This also gave French-speaking Switzerland an important federal institution.
15708.m: The Federal Supreme Court has its seat in Lausanne.

15709.q: What did the Federal Constitution of 1874 require for primary school teaching?
a: It had to be compulsory, free and religiously neutral.
It had to be given by monasteries.
It was only intended for boys.
It had to be in German in all cantons.
15709.e: The cantons remained responsible for schools but had to guarantee adequate primary teaching under state control. This limited the church’s influence on schools.
15709.m: Since 1874 primary school has been compulsory and free.

15710.q: To which wider context do the church policy articles of the 1874 constitution belong?
a: The Kulturkampf between the state and the Catholic Church
15710.e: After the dogma of papal infallibility in 1870, the conflict with the Catholic Church grew sharper. The 1874 constitution, for example, banned new monasteries and required approval for new dioceses.
15710.m: The 1874 constitution was shaped by the Kulturkampf.

15711.q: Which change in marriage law did the Federal Constitution of 1874 introduce?
a: Marriage only from the age of 30
15711.e: Getting married became a matter for the state, and the right to marry was guaranteed. This was part of separating the tasks of state and church.
15711.m: Since 1874 marriages have been concluded before the state.

15712.q: How did the Federal Constitution of 1874 change military affairs?
a: The federal government got more powers over training and weapons.
Each canton was allowed its own navy.
15712.e: The Franco-Prussian War of 1870/71 had shown weaknesses in the cantonal troops. Training and equipment were therefore largely centralised at federal level.
15712.m: The 1874 constitution strengthened the federal role in the army.

15713.q: Which federal law protecting workers was narrowly accepted in a referendum in 1877?
15713.e: The federal Factory Act limited working hours, among other things, and restricted child labour. It was an early example of federal social policy.
15713.m: The Factory Act of 1877 protected workers.

15714.q: How long did the Federal Constitution of 1874 remain in force?
15714.e: It was often partially revised over more than 100 years. On 1 January 2000 the new Federal Constitution of 18 April 1999 replaced it.

15715.q: Which punishment did the Federal Constitution of 1874 abolish in civil criminal law?
15715.e: The 1874 constitution banned the death penalty outside military criminal law. As early as 1879, after a narrow popular vote, the cantons were allowed to bring it back for non-political crimes.
15715.m: The 1874 constitution abolished the death penalty for a time.

15716.q: Which principle of economic life was laid down in the Federal Constitution of 1874?
15716.e: In principle, anyone could run a business anywhere in the country. Cantonal restrictions from the time of the guilds were greatly reduced.
15716.m: The 1874 constitution guaranteed freedom of trade and industry.

15717.q: Which fundamental right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 guarantee more fully than that of 1848?
a: Election of judges by the people
15717.e: In 1848 only the worship of the recognised Christian denominations was protected. The 1874 constitution declared freedom of belief and conscience inviolable.
15717.m: Since 1874 the Federal Constitution has guaranteed freedom of belief and conscience.

15718.q: What could voters do with the “veto” that St Gallen introduced in 1831?
15718.e: With the veto a law could be stopped if enough citizens were against it. It was an early form of the legislative referendum.
15718.m: The veto was a forerunner of the legislative referendum.

15719.q: What did the Democratic Movement of the 1860s demand in cantons such as Zurich?
a: More direct popular rights instead of purely representative government
A return to rule by the patricians
15719.e: The Democrats criticised the “Escher system”, the power of a small liberal elite. They demanded the referendum, the initiative and election of the government by the people.
15719.m: The Democratic Movement demanded more direct popular rights.

15720.q: Which canton adopted a constitution with far-reaching direct democratic rights in 1869?
15720.e: On 18 April 1869 the people of Zurich adopted the new constitution. Among other things it brought the mandatory legislative referendum and the popular initiative.
15720.m: The Zurich constitution of 1869 became a model for direct democracy.

15721.q: Which popular right was introduced at federal level in 1891?
a: The popular initiative for partial revision of the constitution
15721.e: Since 1891 voters have been able to demand a change to individual articles of the constitution. Before that, only an initiative for total revision was possible.
15721.m: The popular initiative for partial revision has existed since 1891.

15722.q: Which popular initiative was the first to be accepted in Switzerland, in 1893?
a: A ban on slaughtering animals without stunning them first
Proportional election of the National Council
15722.e: The ban on slaughter without stunning (shechita) was accepted on 20 August 1893. Researchers also see the vote as an expression of antisemitic attitudes of the time.
15722.m: The first accepted popular initiative, in 1893, concerned ritual slaughter.

15723.q: How many signatures does a federal popular initiative need today?
15723.e: The signatures must be collected within 18 months of publication in the Federal Gazette. To be accepted, it needs a majority of the people and of the cantons.
15723.m: A popular initiative today needs 100,000 signatures.

15724.q: How does an optional referendum against a federal law come about today?
a: With 50,000 signatures or eight cantons within 100 days
With the approval of the Federal Council
15724.e: The deadline starts when the act is published. If the referendum succeeds, only the popular majority decides.
15724.m: A referendum today needs 50,000 signatures or eight cantons.

15725.q: Why were the numbers of signatures for referendums and initiatives raised in 1977?
a: Because of population growth and women’s right to vote
Because of a ban by the Council of Europe
Because there were too few votes
Because the cantons lost their vote
15725.e: Since 1971 women had also been allowed to vote, which roughly doubled the number of voters. The required numbers of signatures were therefore raised.
15725.m: With more voters, the numbers of signatures were raised in 1977.

15726.q: What does the majority of the cantons mean in a vote on the Federal Constitution?
a: Most of the cantons must agree.
The Council of States must agree unanimously.
At least two thirds of the people must agree.
The Federal Council decides if there is a tie.
15726.e: Constitutional changes need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons. The result of the vote in each canton counts as that canton’s vote.
15726.m: Constitutional changes need a majority of the people and of the cantons.

15727.q: Which electoral reform did a popular initiative bring in in 1918, greatly changing the party system?
a: Proportional election of the National Council
Election of the Federal Council by the people
Abolition of the Council of States
15727.e: After proportional representation was introduced, the Free Democrats lost their absolute majority in the National Council in 1919. The Social Democrats and the Farmers’ Party made clear gains.
15727.m: Proportional representation ended the Free Democrats’ majority in the National Council in 1919.

15728.q: Which popular right was added in 1921?
a: The referendum against certain international treaties
The popular initiative for partial revision
15728.e: Since 1921 important treaties under international law can be put to the people. This right was later extended several times.
15728.m: Since 1921 the people can also vote on international treaties.

15729.q: What did the initiative “Return to direct democracy”, narrowly accepted in 1949, want?
a: To limit the emergency powers of parliament and the Federal Council
To introduce women’s right to vote
To have federal judges elected by the people
15729.e: During the crisis and the war, the Federal Council and parliament had declared many decisions urgent, so no referendum could be held on them. The initiative restored the popular rights.
15729.m: The 1949 initiative strengthened popular rights against emergency law.

15730.q: Which canton had to introduce women’s right to vote at cantonal level in 1990 because of a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court?
15730.e: The men at the Landsgemeinde had rejected women’s right to vote several times. On 27 November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that this violated the equality guaranteed in the Federal Constitution.
15730.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce women’s right to vote, in 1990.

15731.q: What does the “double yes” with a deciding question, introduced in 1987, allow?
a: You can vote for an initiative and the counter-proposal at the same time.
You may vote twice on the same proposal.
The Federal Council can overrule a no from the people.
Two cantons can call a referendum together.
15731.e: Before that, supporters of a reform had to choose between the initiative and the counter-proposal, which could weaken both. The deciding question settles which proposal applies if both get a yes.
15731.m: Since 1987 you can accept an initiative and the counter-proposal at the same time.

15732.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin in the second half of the 18th century?
15732.e: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain from around 1750. Coal, capital, colonial trade and modern agriculture created favourable conditions there.
15732.m: Industrialisation began in Great Britain and spread from there to the continent.

15733.q: Which invention by James Watt is considered a key technology of the Industrial Revolution?
15733.e: From 1769 James Watt greatly improved the steam engine so that it needed much less coal. It could then power factories, mines and later locomotives.
15733.m: Watt's steam engine drove the Industrial Revolution.

15734.q: Which development in English agriculture freed up many workers for the factories?
a: The emancipation of the peasants by Napoleon
The introduction of the three-field system
15734.e: Crop rotation, better breeding and the enclosure of common land increased yields. At the same time many farm labourers lost their livelihood and moved to the towns.
15734.m: The Agricultural Revolution provided food and workers for industrialisation.

15735.q: Which fuel replaced scarce charcoal for smelting iron in England in the 18th century?
15735.e: From 1709 coke was used in blast furnaces in England. Iron production was then no longer dependent on scarce wood, and iron became cheaper.
15735.m: Smelting with coke made iron cheaper and independent of charcoal.

15736.q: Which raw material was plentiful and easy to reach in England and helped industrialisation?
15736.e: England had rich coal deposits close to rivers and coasts. Coal supplied the energy for steam engines and blast furnaces.
15736.m: Coal was the most important source of energy of the Industrial Revolution.

15737.q: Why do people speak of a ‘revolution’ even though the change took decades?
a: Because the economy and society were fundamentally transformed
Because it began with the overthrow of a king
Because it happened within a single year
15737.e: The term was coined with the French Revolution in mind. It means the far-reaching upheaval of production, work and ways of life, not a political overthrow.
15737.m: The Industrial Revolution was a long but far-reaching upheaval.

15738.q: What characterises the so-called Second Industrial Revolution from the late 19th century?
a: The steam engine and the spinning machine
The water wheel and the windmill
15738.e: From around 1870 electricity, chemistry and new production methods became important, and later the assembly line too. The term Second Industrial Revolution was coined in 1936 by the sociologist Georges Friedmann.
15738.m: The Second Industrial Revolution was based on electricity and mass production.

15739.q: Which period is usually considered the core phase of the Industrial Revolution in Great Britain?
15739.e: Historians usually date the Industrial Revolution in Great Britain to about 1750 to 1850. Other countries followed later, for example Germany and Switzerland in the 19th century.
15739.m: British industrialisation falls roughly between 1750 and 1850.

15740.q: Who had the first practically proven piston steam engine for pumping water set up in an English coal mine in 1712?
15740.e: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine was installed in a mine in Staffordshire in 1712. It pumped water reliably but had an efficiency of only about 0.5 per cent.
15740.m: Newcomen's engine of 1712 was the first piston steam engine proven in mining.

15741.q: What were the early steam engines mainly used for?
15741.e: Mines kept filling up with water. The first steam engines were therefore used as pumps before they later powered factories and vehicles.
15741.m: The steam engine first helped mining to dig deeper for coal.

15742.q: Which decisive improvement did James Watt patent in 1769?
a: A condenser separate from the cylinder
A safety valve for cooking pots
15742.e: Watt moved the condensing of the steam into a separate container. His patent dates from 1769.
15742.m: With the separate condenser James Watt made the steam engine much more efficient.

15743.q: Which engineer first ran a steam locomotive on rails in Wales in 1804?
15743.e: Richard Trevithick relied on high-pressure steam, which allowed smaller and lighter engines. On 21 February 1804 his locomotive pulled a load on rails at the Pen-y-Darren ironworks.
15743.m: Trevithick's high-pressure engine made the steam locomotive possible.

15744.q: With which businessman did James Watt market his steam engines?
15744.e: Matthew Boulton was Watt's business partner. The firm of Boulton & Watt sold the improved engines successfully.
15744.m: Only the partnership with Matthew Boulton brought Watt's invention to market.

15745.q: Which unit of power did James Watt use to compare his engines with working animals?
15745.e: Watt compared the power of his engines with the work of horses. This way buyers could judge how many animals an engine replaced.
15745.m: Horsepower served as a clear comparison for the power of steam engines.

15746.q: What effect did the steam engine have on where factories were located?
a: Factories were no longer tied to water power
Factories now had to stand by waterfalls
Factories were moved into the mountains
Factories were only allowed in the countryside
15746.e: Before, factories needed water wheels on rivers. With the steam engine they could be built where coal, workers and markets were, often in towns.
15746.m: The steam engine made factories independent of rivers.

15747.q: Which physicist presented a steam pressure cooker in 1679 and in 1690 described an early piston model seen as a forerunner of the steam engine?
15747.e: Denis Papin's pressure cooker of 1679 only worked safely with the safety valve he invented. In 1690 he described a cylinder with a piston that was moved by heating and cooling water.
15747.m: Denis Papin was one of the early pioneers of steam technology.

15748.q: Which invention by John Kay in 1733 speeded up weaving?
15748.e: With the flying shuttle a weaver could weave faster and make wider cloth. Soon there was not enough yarn, which made spinning machines necessary.
15748.m: The flying shuttle made weaving faster than spinning.

15749.q: Which spinning machine did James Hargreaves invent around 1764?
15749.e: The spinning jenny could spin with many spindles at the same time. Hargreaves patented it in 1770.
15749.m: The spinning jenny multiplied the amount of yarn a single spinner could make.

15750.q: What is Richard Arkwright's water-powered spinning mill in Cromford considered a model for?
a: The modern factory with many machines in one place
The putting-out system with home workers
15750.e: From 1771 many people in Cromford worked in fixed shifts at machines driven by a water wheel. This model was copied many times.
15750.m: Arkwright's mill in Cromford is an early model of the modern factory.

15751.q: Which machine did Samuel Crompton develop in 1779 by combining the spinning jenny and the water frame?
15751.e: The spinning mule combined the advantages of both machines. It produced yarn that was both fine and strong.
15751.m: Crompton's spinning mule produced fine and strong yarn.

15752.q: Who invented the power loom in 1784?
15752.e: Edmund Cartwright developed a mechanical loom in 1784, and a prototype followed the next year. Later it was powered by steam.
15752.m: With Cartwright's loom weaving was mechanised too.

15753.q: Which invention by Eli Whitney (1793) made cotton growing in the southern United States, and with it slave labour, grow greatly?
15753.e: The cotton gin separated cotton fibres from the seeds much faster. Growing cotton became even more profitable, and the number of enslaved people on plantations rose.
15753.m: The cotton gin closely linked the textile industry with slavery in the USA.

15754.q: Why was the cotton industry the pioneer of mechanisation?
a: Great demand and fibres that were easy to process by machine
Cotton grew in large quantities in England
Wool could no longer be processed
15754.e: Cheap cotton fabrics were in great demand, and raw cotton came cheaply from overseas. The fibres were easy to spin with machines.
15754.m: Cotton was the leading sector of early industrialisation.

15755.q: Which uprising in 1844 showed the hardship of hand weavers facing competition from machines?
15755.e: The Silesian weavers suffered from falling prices caused by machine-made cloth. Their uprising of 1844 was crushed by the army.
15755.m: The weavers' uprising of 1844 made the social hardship of home workers visible.

15756.q: What was meant by the truck system in the early factory age?
a: Paying workers in goods or vouchers instead of money
Working in alternating day and night shifts
15756.e: Under the truck system workers received all or part of their wages in goods or vouchers, often at inflated prices. In Great Britain Truck Acts restricted this practice from 1831, and Prussia banned it in 1849.
15756.m: The truck system made workers even more dependent on their employer.

15757.q: How did the putting-out system, which came before the factory, work?
a: A merchant supplied raw materials to home workers and sold the goods
A publisher printed books for workers
Workers set up a cooperative together
15757.e: The merchant provided raw materials and took the finished products. The work was done at home, often as a second income in the countryside.
15757.m: In the putting-out system people worked at home for an entrepreneur.

15758.q: Why did many of the first factories in the 18th century stand by rivers?
a: The goods were only sold by raft
River water cooled the electric motors
15758.e: Early factories such as the silk mill in Derby or Arkwright's mill in Cromford used water power. Only the steam engine made them independent of rivers.
15758.m: The first factories used water power and so stood by rivers.

15759.q: What was typical of work discipline in early factories?
a: Fixed hours, factory rules and penalties for being late
An eight-hour day with paid holidays
15759.e: The machines set the pace. Factory rules governed hours and behaviour, and breaking them was punished with wage deductions or dismissal.
15759.m: In the factory the clock, no longer the season, set the rhythm of work.

15760.q: Roughly how long was a working day in many early factories?
15760.e: Working days of 12 hours and more were normal, six days a week. Only factory laws limited working hours step by step.
15760.m: Long working days were one of the greatest burdens of early factory work.

15761.q: Which factory owner introduced reforms such as a school for workers' children at the New Lanark mill in Scotland?
15761.e: Robert Owen shortened working hours at New Lanark and set up a school. He is seen as an early social reformer and pioneer of the cooperative movement.
15761.m: Robert Owen showed at New Lanark that a factory could also be run in a socially responsible way.

15762.q: What is meant by the division of labour in a factory?
a: Breaking production down into many simple steps
Sharing the wages among all workers
Dividing the factory among several owners
15762.e: Each worker does only one small, repetitive step. This increases productivity but makes the work monotonous.
15762.m: The division of labour increased production but made work monotonous.

15763.q: What were the workers called who destroyed machines in protest in England from 1811?
15763.e: The Luddites referred to a legendary, probably invented leader called Ned Ludd. They destroyed machines because they feared for their jobs and wages.
15763.m: The machine breakers fought against losing their livelihood to machines.

15764.q: Which railway in England, opened in 1825, is considered the first public railway with steam locomotives?
15764.e: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825. At first both locomotives and horses pulled the trains there.
15764.m: The railway age began in 1825 with the Stockton and Darlington Railway.

15765.q: Which locomotive by Robert Stephenson won the Rainhill Trials in 1829?
15765.e: In 1829 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway was looking for a suitable locomotive. Rocket impressed in the tests and became the model for later steam locomotives.
15765.m: In 1829 Rocket proved that steam locomotives could run reliably.

15766.q: When was the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, the first railway run entirely by steam between two large cities, opened?
15766.e: The line opened on 15 September 1830. It linked the port of Liverpool with the textile city of Manchester.
15766.m: The railway from Liverpool to Manchester opened the age of modern rail travel in 1830.

15767.q: When did the first German railway run between Nuremberg and Fürth with the locomotive ‘Adler’?
15767.e: The Ludwig Railway opened on 7 December 1835. The locomotive ‘Adler’ came from Robert Stephenson's company.
15767.m: Germany's railway age began in 1835 with the ‘Adler’.

15768.q: Why is the railway considered the engine of heavy industry?
a: It needed huge amounts of coal, iron and steel
It replaced coal with water power
It needed only wood as building material
15768.e: Rails, locomotives and bridges needed a lot of iron and steel, and running them needed a lot of coal. At the same time the railway lowered transport costs for all goods.
15768.m: The railway was both a customer and a driving force of heavy industry.

15769.q: Which change in timekeeping did the railway encourage?
a: Standard time zones instead of local times
The invention of the atomic clock
The abolition of the days of the week
15769.e: Reliable timetables needed a standard time. So local solar times were replaced by railway time and later by time zones.
15769.m: Timetables required a single time across large areas.

15770.q: When was the first railway running entirely on Swiss soil, from Zurich to Baden, opened?
15770.e: The Swiss Northern Railway opened the line of about 23 km on 7 August 1847. It is popularly known as the ‘Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn’ (‘Spanish Bun Railway’).
15770.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn of 1847 was the first railway within Switzerland.

15771.q: To whom did the Swiss Railway Act of 1852 leave the building of railways?
15771.e: The act of 1852 left railway building to private companies with cantonal concessions. This led to competition and in places to parallel lines.
15771.m: In Switzerland private companies built the first railways.

15772.q: What did Swiss voters decide about the railways on 20 February 1898?
a: The buying back of the large private railways by the Confederation
The building of the Gotthard Base Tunnel
The privatisation of the post office
15772.e: The people approved the nationalisation of the five large private railways. This created the SBB (Swiss Federal Railways), which began operating on 1 January 1902.
15772.m: The nationalisation of 1898 led to the founding of the SBB.

15773.q: With which industry did the industrialisation of Switzerland begin around 1800?
15773.e: In 1801 in St Gallen and 1802 in Winterthur the first mechanical spinning machines on the English model were set up. This began the mechanisation of the Swiss textile industry.
15773.m: Swiss industrialisation began shortly after 1800 with spinning machines.

15774.q: Who founded a company in Zurich in 1805 from which the engineering firm Escher Wyss developed?
15774.e: Hans Caspar Escher first built spinning machines. The firm became a major maker of turbines, ships and machines.
15774.m: In Switzerland mechanical engineering grew out of the textile industry.

15775.q: Why was Switzerland able to industrialise early even though it had hardly any coal?
a: Water power, a tradition of home work and a focus on exports
Large coal and iron deposits of its own
Raw materials from its own colonies
15775.e: Rivers provided energy for factories, and many people had experience from home work. Swiss firms specialised in high-quality export products.
15775.m: In Switzerland water power and a focus on exports made up for the lack of coal.

15776.q: What happened in Oberuster on 22 November 1832?
a: Home workers set fire to a mechanical spinning and weaving mill
The first trade union was founded
A factory law came into force
15776.e: In the Uster fire, home workers and small manufacturers from the Zurich Oberland set fire to the Corrodi & Pfister mechanical spinning and weaving mill. They feared the weaving machines would destroy their livelihood.
15776.m: The Uster fire of 1832 was the best-known case of machine breaking in Switzerland.

15777.q: Which canton passed a progressive factory law in 1864 that became a model for the Confederation?
15777.e: In 1864 Glarus introduced a factory law with a twelve-hour day. It is seen as an important forerunner of the federal Factory Act of 1877.
15777.m: The Glarus factory law of 1864 paved the way for protecting factory workers.

15778.q: Which maximum daily working time did the federal Factory Act of 1877 set?
15778.e: The Factory Act of 1877 limited work to 11 hours a day, that is 65 hours a week. It was narrowly accepted in a referendum.
15778.m: The Factory Act of 1877 introduced the eleven-hour day throughout Switzerland.

15779.q: Which bank did Alfred Escher found in 1856, mainly to finance railways?
15779.e: Railway building needed a lot of capital. For this purpose Alfred Escher founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt in 1856.
15779.m: Banks such as the Kreditanstalt financed Swiss railway building.

15780.q: Which industry especially shaped eastern Switzerland around St Gallen in the 19th century?
15780.e: Around 1900 St Gallen embroidery was one of Switzerland's most important export industries. Much embroidery was made by home workers and in factories.
15780.m: Embroidery made St Gallen a world-famous textile centre.

15781.q: Which electrical engineering company was founded in Baden in 1891?
15781.e: Charles Brown and Walter Boveri founded BBC in Baden in 1891. It built generators, turbines and electrical equipment.
15781.m: With BBC Switzerland also became important in the electrical industry.

15782.q: In which year was the Gotthard Railway with the Gotthard Tunnel opened along its whole length?
15782.e: Through traffic on the Gotthard Railway began on 1 June 1882. The tunnel links Göschenen and Airolo.
15782.m: Since 1882 the railway has run through the Gotthard.

15783.q: On which day did the breakthrough in the Gotthard Tunnel happen?
15783.e: On 29 February 1880 the miners from the north and south met inside the mountain. Construction had begun in 1872.
15783.m: The breakthrough in the Gotthard happened on a leap day in 1880.

15784.q: Which Geneva building contractor led the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel and died in the tunnel in 1879?
15784.e: Louis Favre died of heart failure on 19 July 1879 during an inspection in the tunnel. He did not live to see the breakthrough.
15784.m: Louis Favre built the Gotthard Tunnel but did not live to see it completed.

15785.q: Roughly how long is the Gotthard summit tunnel of 1882?
15785.e: The tunnel is about 15 km long. At the time it was the longest railway tunnel in the world.
15785.m: The Gotthard Tunnel of 1882 is about 15 kilometres long.

15786.q: What happened in July 1875 during the tunnel workers' strike in Göschenen?
a: A police unit fired into the crowd and four workers died
The workers immediately won higher wages
The tunnel was shut down for ten years
The workers elected their own site managers
15786.e: The workers went on strike against dangerous conditions and low wages. On 27 July 1875 a police unit fired into the crowd, and four Italian workers were killed.
15786.m: The Göschenen strike of 1875 ended in bloodshed and showed the harsh conditions of tunnel building.

15787.q: Which countries besides Switzerland helped to finance the Gotthard Railway?
15787.e: In the Gotthard Treaty of 1871 Italy and Germany promised large subsidies, and in 1878 further contributions were added because of extra costs. Both countries wanted a fast north-south link through the Alps.
15787.m: The Gotthard Railway was an international project with money from Italy and Germany.

15788.q: Which tunnel, about 57 km long, has been in operation since 2016 and runs much deeper under the Gotthard massif?
15788.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel was opened in 2016 and is about 57 km long. It allows a flat route without steep gradients.
15788.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel of 2016 adds to the old summit tunnel of 1882.

15789.q: How do specialists distinguish between the growth of cities and urbanisation?
a: The growth of cities means cities getting bigger; urbanisation also includes urban ways of life
Both terms mean exactly the same
The growth of cities concerns only villages, urbanisation only capitals
15789.e: The growth of cities mainly describes their spreading out and their population growth. Urbanisation also includes the spread of urban ways of life.
15789.m: Urbanisation is more than just cities getting bigger.

15790.q: What was a main cause of the growth of cities in the 19th century?
a: Rural exodus because of population growth and factory work
15790.e: In the countryside there was not enough land and work for the growing population. In the towns factories attracted people with paid work.
15790.m: Many people moved to the towns because the factories there offered work.

15791.q: Which disease spread in cities in the 19th century mainly through dirty drinking water?
15791.e: Cholera is transmitted by contaminated water. The crowded, badly drained workers' districts were especially affected.
15791.m: Cholera epidemics showed how urgently cities needed clean water.

15792.q: Which infrastructure became especially necessary in industrial cities because of dense settlement?
a: Sewers and a central water supply
15792.e: More people in a small space produced more sewage and increased the risk of epidemics. Cities therefore built sewers and water pipes.
15792.m: Sewers and clean water greatly improved health in the cities.

15793.q: Since when, according to the United Nations, has more than half of the world's population lived in cities?
15793.e: Around 1950 about 70 per cent of people lived in the countryside. Since about 2008 more than half of the world's population has lived in cities.
15793.m: The growth of cities continues worldwide today.

15794.q: Which English industrial city did Friedrich Engels study for his description of workers' districts?
15794.e: Engels lived in England for about 21 months, mainly in Manchester. There he observed housing conditions and the separation of districts by social class.
15794.m: Manchester became the symbol of the growing industrial city.

a: Densely built, multi-storey rented buildings for workers' families
15795.e: Especially in Berlin, large tenement buildings with several back courtyards were built. Many people lived there in very cramped conditions, often with little light.
15795.m: Tenement blocks stand for the cramped housing of the working class.

15796.q: What happened to the city of Zurich in 1893?
a: It grew greatly by taking in eleven suburbs
It became the federal city of Switzerland
15796.e: In 1893 eleven neighbouring municipalities such as Aussersihl, Enge and Wipkingen were incorporated. The fast-growing workers' suburbs could hardly manage their tasks on their own any more.
15796.m: The incorporation of 1893 made Zurich grow greatly in one go.

15797.q: Which innovation in the British Factory Act of 1833 made sure that the rules on child labour were actually enforced?
a: A trade union for factory children
A special tax on child labour
15797.e: Earlier laws of 1802 and 1819 were hardly checked. The Factory Act of 1833 created a state factory inspectorate whose inspectors could enter workplaces and punish breaches.
15797.m: Only state inspectors made the protection of factory children effective.

15798.q: From what age were children allowed to work in textile factories under the British Factory Act of 1833?
15798.e: Children under nine could no longer be employed, except in silk mills. For children aged 9 to 13 a maximum working time of 8 hours a day applied.
15798.m: The Factory Act of 1833 banned factory work for children under nine.

15799.q: For which children did the federal Factory Act of 1877 ban factory work?
15799.e: The Factory Act of 1877 banned work in factories for children under 14. It also banned night work for women and young people.
15799.m: Since 1877 children under 14 have not been allowed to work in factories in Switzerland.

15800.q: Why did Prussia restrict child labour in 1839?
a: Child labour prevented school attendance and weakened future recruits
The factories had too many adult workers
The Church banned all work by children
Great Britain demanded it in a treaty
15800.e: The Prussian regulation of 1839 banned factory work for children under nine. The reason was that child labour prevented school attendance; the army also complained about too few healthy recruits.
15800.m: Prussia began protecting working children in 1839.

a: Children from Alpine regions who worked in Upper Swabia in summer
Children who lived in mines in Swabia
15801.e: Children from Tyrol, Vorarlberg, Liechtenstein and Switzerland walked to Upper Swabia in spring. There they worked for farmers over the summer until the early 20th century.
15801.m: The Swabian children show that child labour was also widespread in farming.

a: Children who were placed with other families and often had to do hard work
Children who did an apprenticeship in factories
Children of rich families at boarding school
15802.e: From about 1800 into the 1960s, orphans, children of divorced parents and children of poor families were mostly placed on farms. Many had to work hard without pay and suffered mistreatment; in 2013 the Federal Council apologised to those affected.
15802.m: The fate of the contract children is a dark chapter of Swiss social history.

15803.q: Why did many factory owners in the 19th century like to employ children?
a: They got very low wages and were considered obedient
They were better trained than adults
They only worked a short time each day
15803.e: Children got only a fraction of an adult's wage. Their strength was enough for many simple jobs at machines, and they rarely fought back.
15803.m: Child labour was cheap for factory owners and often vital for the survival of poor families.

15804.q: Which UN organisation works worldwide with conventions against child labour?
15804.e: The ILO, based in Geneva, draws up conventions against child labour. It also created the World Day Against Child Labour on 12 June.
15804.m: The ILO in Geneva fights child labour worldwide.

15805.q: What is meant by the ‘social question’ in the 19th century?
a: The hardship of the working class through poverty, housing shortage and lack of security
The question of voting rights for nobles
The dispute over the state religion
15805.e: Industrialisation and population growth brought mass poverty, bad housing and insecure work. The question of how to solve these problems was called the social question.
15805.m: The social question was the great challenge of industrial society.

15806.q: What does the term pauperism mean?
a: Mass poverty in the early 19th century
15806.e: Pauperism refers to the widespread poverty before and at the start of industrialisation. Many people could hardly make a living even though they worked.
15806.m: Pauperism shows that poverty was widespread even before the factories.

15807.q: Which social insurance did Otto von Bismarck introduce first in the German Empire in 1883?
15807.e: Health insurance came in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and invalidity and old-age insurance in 1889. Germany thus became a pioneer of state social insurance.
15807.m: In 1883 Bismarck began building the welfare state with health insurance.

15808.q: Besides helping workers, which political aim did Bismarck pursue with his social legislation?
a: To keep the workers away from social democracy
To promote free trade with England
15808.e: At the same time Bismarck suppressed the Social Democrats with the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878. This is why it is called a carrot-and-stick policy.
15808.m: Bismarck's social policy was meant to bind the workers to the state.

15809.q: With which encyclical did Pope Leo XIII take a position on the social question in 1891?
15809.e: In ‘Rerum Novarum’ Leo XIII called for fair wages and allowed workers' associations. The encyclical is seen as the foundation of Catholic social teaching.
15809.m: With ‘Rerum Novarum’ the Catholic Church responded to the workers' question in 1891.

15810.q: Which work about the working class did Friedrich Engels publish in 1845?
a: The Condition of the Working Class in England
15810.e: In 1845 Engels described living and working conditions in English industrial cities. It was based on his own observations and official reports.
15810.m: In 1845 Engels made the hardship of English workers known throughout Europe.

15811.q: How did some factory owners respond to the social question as part of so-called employer paternalism?
a: They built workers' housing estates and provided company doctors
They handed the factories over to the workers
15811.e: Some employers provided housing, funds and doctors for their workforce. They combined care with control and strict discipline.
15811.m: Employer paternalism combined social care with control over the workers.

15812.q: Which Catholic priest founded associations that offered travelling journeymen lodging and education?
15812.e: Adolph Kolping founded the Cologne Journeymen's Association in 1849 and from 1850 linked further associations into a federation. They gave travelling journeymen support, education and community.
15812.m: Church associations such as Kolping's also looked for answers to the social question.

15813.q: Which work did Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish in February 1848?
a: The Condition of the Working Class in England
15813.e: The Manifesto was written on behalf of the Communist League. It called for the workers' class struggle against the bourgeoisie.
15813.m: The Communist Manifesto of 1848 became a key text of the labour movement.

15814.q: With which call does the Communist Manifesto end?
a: One for all, all for one!
15814.e: The closing call stresses the international solidarity of the workers. It became the best-known slogan of the socialist movement.
15814.m: From the start, the labour movement saw itself as international.

15815.q: What was the aim of the First International, founded in 1864?
a: To link workers' organisations from different countries
To create free trade between the great powers
To care for wounded soldiers in war
15815.e: The International Workingmen's Association was founded in London in 1864. As a member of the General Council, Karl Marx wrote its programme texts.
15815.m: From 1864 the First International linked workers' associations from many countries.

15816.q: What did the Chartists in England mainly demand?
a: Universal and equal suffrage for men
15816.e: The Chartists were named after their ‘People's Charter’. They fought with petitions and mass meetings for workers to have a political say.
15816.m: The Chartists combined social concerns with the demand for the vote.

15817.q: When did the Swiss Workers' Congress decide to found the Social Democratic Party of Switzerland?
15817.e: The founding of the SP was decided on 21 October 1888. Albert Steck wrote the party programme.
15817.m: The Swiss SP has existed since 1888 as the political voice of the labour movement.

15818.q: Which organisation was founded in Geneva in 1838 with the motto ‘Through education to freedom’?
15818.e: The Grütli Association was at first an educational association for journeymen. Later it became political and joined the SP in 1901.
15818.m: The Grütli Association is one of the oldest workers' organisations in Switzerland.

15819.q: Which committee called the general strike in Switzerland in November 1918?
15819.e: The Olten Action Committee under Robert Grimm brought together the SP and the trade unions. The general strike lasted from 12 to 14 November 1918, and around 250,000 people took part.
15819.m: The general strike of 1918 was the most serious domestic crisis of the federal state.

15820.q: Which demand of the general strike was already put into practice in 1919?
a: Election of the National Council by proportional representation
15820.e: Proportional representation had already been approved by the people in October 1918 and was first used in 1919. The AHV only came in 1948 and women's suffrage in 1971.
15820.m: Several demands of the general strike later came true, proportional representation first.

15821.q: What happened in Grenchen on 14 November 1918 during the general strike?
a: Soldiers shot three young watch workers
The strikers took over the town government
15821.e: During an army deployment in Grenchen, shots were fired at demonstrators. Three watch workers aged 17, 21 and 29 died.
15821.m: The dead of Grenchen recall how hard the conflict of 1918 was.

15822.q: In which year was the Swiss Trade Union Federation founded in Olten?
15822.e: The Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB) was founded in 1880 in the station buffet in Olten. It is still the largest umbrella organisation of Swiss trade unions.
15822.m: Since 1880 the SGB has represented the interests of employees in Switzerland.

15823.q: Which trade union was formed in 2004 by merging several unions such as GBI and SMUV and is now the largest in Switzerland?
15823.e: Unia was formed on 16 October 2004 from the merger of unions from construction, industry, trades and services. It has about 180,000 members.
15823.m: Unia is now the largest trade union in Switzerland.

15824.q: When was the so-called Peace Agreement signed in the engineering and metal industry?
15824.e: The Peace Agreement was signed in Zurich on 19 July 1937. It is seen as the basis of the Swiss social partnership.
15824.m: The Peace Agreement of 1937 founded industrial peace in Switzerland.

15825.q: Which trade unionist signed the Peace Agreement of 1937 for the employees' side?
15825.e: Konrad Ilg of the Metal and Watch Workers' Union signed for the trade unions. Ernst Dübi signed for the employers.
15825.m: Konrad Ilg and Ernst Dübi stand for the start of the social partnership.

15826.q: What does the ‘absolute peace obligation’ in the Peace Agreement of 1937 mean?
a: Giving up strikes and lockouts while the agreement is in force
A ban on the army at home
A duty to take part in peace demonstrations
A ban on trade unions in wartime
15826.e: Both sides gave up industrial action. Instead, conflicts were to be settled in a multi-stage arbitration procedure.
15826.m: The peace obligation replaces industrial action with negotiation.

15827.q: What is a collective labour agreement (GAV)?
a: An agreement between employers and trade unions on wages and working conditions
An employment contract between two individuals
A Federal Council law on holidays
A contract to buy a factory
15827.e: A collective labour agreement sets wages, working hours and holidays for a whole industry or company. In 1974 the Peace Agreement of 1937 was developed into a full collective labour agreement.
15827.m: Collective labour agreements are a key tool of the social partnership.

15828.q: Which measure do employers use against a strike by temporarily shutting workers out of the workplace?
15828.e: In a lockout the employer does not let the employees work and pays no wages. It is the counterpart to the strike.
15828.m: Strikes and lockouts are the classic means of industrial action.

15829.q: Why were Christian trade unions also founded in Switzerland alongside the SGB?
a: Many workers wanted a non-socialist, religiously based representation
The SGB did not accept Swiss people
The state banned the SGB completely for a time
Christian trade unions represented only employers
15829.e: Catholic and Protestant workers founded their own unions, such as the Christian Metal Workers' Union. They too signed the Peace Agreement of 1937.
15829.m: For a long time Swiss trade unions were divided by world view.

15830.q: Which period do historians usually call ‘high imperialism’?
15830.e: High imperialism is the period from about 1870 to the First World War. In these decades the European powers divided almost all of Africa and large parts of Asia among themselves.
15830.m: High imperialism lasted from about 1870 to 1914.

15831.q: Which Latin word does the term ‘imperialism’ come from?
15831.e: ‘Imperium’ means power of command or area of rule, and the verb ‘imperare’ means to rule. The term imperialism refers to the striving for rule over foreign territories.
15831.m: The word imperialism comes from the Latin ‘imperium’.

a: Economic and political domination of formally independent states
The direct administration of a colony by officials
The settlement of an area by farmers from Europe
The union of colonies into a federal state
15832.e: In informal imperialism a country remains formally sovereign but is made economically and politically dependent on a great power. One example is China in the 19th century.
15832.m: Informal imperialism dominates states without officially making them colonies.

15833.q: Which continent was almost completely divided up among European powers in the age of imperialism?
15833.e: Between about 1880 and 1914 the European powers divided almost all of Africa among themselves. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
15833.m: In the age of imperialism almost all of Africa was colonised.

15834.q: How did Lenin describe imperialism in his work of 1916?
a: As the highest stage of capitalism
As a preliminary stage of democracy
15834.e: Lenin's work ‘Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism’ saw monopolies and the export of capital as the driving forces of expansion. He believed this phase was the last stage of capitalism.
15834.m: Lenin saw imperialism as the highest stage of capitalism.

15835.q: Which ideology applied Darwin's idea of the ‘struggle for existence’ to peoples and was used to justify imperialism?
15835.e: Social Darwinism claimed that only ‘strong’ peoples could prevail. This scientifically untenable theory was used to justify conquest and racism.
15835.m: Social Darwinism misused Darwin's ideas to justify conquests.

15836.q: Who wrote the 1899 poem “The White Man's Burden”, which was used to justify colonial rule?
15836.e: In it, Kipling called on the USA to take over rule of the Philippines. The poem presents colonial rule as a supposed “burden” and a civilising task.
15836.m: Rudyard Kipling's 1899 poem glorified colonial rule as a duty of white people.

15837.q: What is the idea called that Europeans had to bring “civilisation” to other peoples, which was used to justify colonial rule?
15837.e: The civilising mission (French “mission civilisatrice”) presented conquest as a kindness. It was based on the assumption that one's own culture was superior.
15837.m: The civilising mission served as a justification for colonial rule.

15838.q: With which slogan did the German state secretary Bernhard von Bülow demand German colonies in 1897?
15838.e: On 6 December 1897 Bülow told the Reichstag that Germany also demanded its “place in the sun”. The phrase became a slogan for Germany's claim to colonies and world standing.
15838.m: With the “place in the sun”, Germany demanded colonies of its own.

15839.q: Which economic motive played a central role in imperialism?
a: Access to raw materials and markets
Abolishing all customs duties in Europe
15839.e: Industrialisation increased the demand for raw materials such as cotton, rubber or copper. Colonies were also meant to serve as markets for industrial goods.
15839.m: Raw materials and new markets were important motives of imperialism.

15840.q: What is the policy called that Wilhelm II pursued at the end of the 19th century to make Germany a world power with colonies and a navy?
15840.e: Wilhelm II broke away from Bismarck's cautious alliance policy and strove for world standing. This included colonies and a large naval build-up, which worsened tensions with Great Britain.
15840.m: German Weltpolitik worsened tensions with Great Britain.

15841.q: Which state acquired the Philippines in 1898 after the war against Spain?
15841.e: After the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded the Philippines to the USA in the Treaty of Paris in 1898. The USA thereby became a colonial power in Asia itself.
15841.m: From 1898 the USA was a colonial power in Asia.

15842.q: Which consequence of imperialism is seen as one of the long-term causes of the First World War?
a: the sharper rivalry between the great powers
the founding of the League of Nations
15842.e: Competition for colonies led to crises such as Fashoda or the Moroccan Crises. These tensions hardened the alliance systems before 1914.
15842.m: Colonial rivalry contributed to the tensions before the First World War.

15843.q: Which domestic aim did governments in the German Empire also pursue with colonial successes?
a: To distract from social tensions at home
To raise taxes for the rich
15843.e: Successes abroad were meant to stir pride and distract from conflicts between workers and property owners. Historians call this social imperialism.
15843.m: Colonial successes were meant to distract from internal conflicts.

15844.q: What is the basic difference between colonialism and imperialism?
a: Colonialism means direct rule over colonies, imperialism any form of expanding power
Colonialism means any form of expanding power, imperialism only rule over settler colonies
Colonialism means only trade with colonies, imperialism only their military conquest
Colonialism means the time before 1800, imperialism the same policy after 1800 with no real difference
15844.e: Colonialism means rule over a territory with a foreign population by a foreign power. Imperialism is broader and also includes indirect domination without colonies.
15844.m: Imperialism is the broader term, colonialism means direct rule.

15845.q: What do you call a colony to which many people from the mother country emigrated permanently?
15845.e: Many Europeans settled in settler colonies such as Australia or Canada. The local population was often pushed out or decimated.
15845.m: Many people from Europe settled in settler colonies.

a: a territory with its own government that is under the control of a foreign protecting power
a colony without a local population
a trading post on the coast
an independent state without an army
15846.e: In a protectorate, local rulers formally stay in office, but the protecting power decides above all foreign and military policy. Examples are Tunisia under France or Zanzibar under Great Britain.
15846.m: A protectorate is under the influence of a foreign protecting power.

15847.q: Which principle of British colonial administration used local rulers and structures to govern a territory?
15847.e: Under indirect rule, the British governed for example Nigeria through local rulers. This saved staff and costs.
15847.m: Under indirect rule, the colonial power governed through local rulers.

15848.q: Which colonial policy did France officially pursue by trying to turn local people into “Frenchmen”?
15848.e: The assimilation policy was meant to spread France's language, culture and law in the colonies. In practice, however, only a small minority received full civil rights.
15848.m: France officially pursued an assimilation policy in its colonies.

15849.q: Which Swiss missionary society was founded in 1815 and worked, among other places, on the Gold Coast (today Ghana)?
15849.e: The Basel Mission was founded in 1815 and worked on the Gold Coast from 1828 and in southern India from 1834. Through its own trading company it also traded in cocoa and palm oil.
15849.m: The Basel Mission worked in Africa and India from the 19th century.

15850.q: In which colonial army did around 8,000 Swiss mercenaries serve between 1815 and the First World War?
a: in the Dutch army in the Dutch East Indies
15850.e: Many Swiss signed up for the Dutch colonial army in what is now Indonesia. This shows that Switzerland took part in colonialism even without colonies of its own.
15850.m: Swiss men also fought as mercenaries in colonial wars.

15851.q: How did Swiss trading houses profit from colonialism in the 19th century, although Switzerland had no colonies?
a: They traded in raw materials from colonies such as cotton and coffee
They bought their own islands in the Caribbean
15851.e: Firms such as Gebrüder Volkart from Winterthur imported cotton and coffee from India and exported industrial goods. In this way Switzerland was closely tied into colonial world trade.
15851.m: Swiss trading houses profited from colonial world trade.

15852.q: How is Switzerland's involvement in colonialism often described by researchers?
