16922.e: The ECSC was founded on 18 April 1951 by Belgium, West Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. It placed coal and steel under common supervision.
16922.m: The Coal and Steel Community of 1951 is seen as the beginning of European unification.

16923.q: Which treaties founded the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom in 1957?
16923.e: The Treaties of Rome were signed on 25 March 1957. They created the EEC and the European Atomic Energy Community.
16923.m: The EEC was created with the Treaties of Rome in 1957.

16924.q: Which treaty founded the European Union and came into force on 1 November 1993?
16924.e: The Maastricht Treaty was signed on 7 February 1992 and came into force in 1993. It founded the EU and set the path to monetary union.
16924.m: The Maastricht Treaty turned the Community into the European Union.

16925.q: How many states joined the EU in the eastern enlargement on 1 May 2004?
16925.e: On 1 May 2004 ten states joined, including Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the three Baltic states. It was the largest enlargement in EU history.
16925.m: The eastern enlargement of 2004 brought the EU ten new members.

16926.q: When was the euro introduced as cash, after already existing as book money from 1999?
16926.e: From 1999 the euro was used as book money for payments. Coins and banknotes came into circulation on 1 January 2002.
16926.m: Euro coins and banknotes have existed since 1 January 2002.

16927.q: On which day did the United Kingdom leave the EU after the 2016 referendum?
16927.e: In the referendum of 23 June 2016 a majority voted to leave. Brexit took place on 31 January 2020, followed by a transition period until the end of 2020.
16927.m: Brexit legally took place on 31 January 2020.

16928.q: How did Swiss voters decide on joining the European Economic Area (EEA) on 6 December 1992?
16928.e: The people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the EEA on 6 December 1992. Switzerland then chose the bilateral path with the EU.
16928.m: After the EEA no of 1992, Switzerland relied on bilateral agreements.

16929.q: When did the Bilateral Agreements I between Switzerland and the EU come into force?
16929.e: The seven agreements of the Bilaterals I were concluded in 1999 and approved by the people on 21 May 2000. They came into force on 1 June 2002.
16929.m: The Bilaterals I have applied since 2002 and include free movement of persons.

16930.q: In which city is the World Trade Organization (WTO) based?
16930.e: The WTO began its work on 1 January 1995 and is based in Geneva. It sets rules for international trade and settles trade disputes.
16930.m: The World Trade Organization is based in Geneva.

16931.q: Which agreement of 1947 was the forerunner of the World Trade Organization?
16931.e: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947 gradually lowered customs duties. After the Uruguay Round it became part of the WTO in 1995.
16931.m: The GATT of 1947 was the forerunner of the WTO.

16932.q: With which agreement, signed in April 1994, was the WTO founded?
16932.e: The Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO was signed in April 1994. It came into force on 1 January 1995.
16932.m: The Marrakesh Agreement created the World Trade Organization in 1994.

16933.q: Which highly populated country joined the WTO in December 2001?
16933.e: China became a member of the WTO in December 2001. Joining greatly strengthened China’s integration into world trade.
16933.m: By joining the WTO in 2001, China became a firm part of world trade.

16934.q: Which invention of the 1950s cut transport costs in world trade particularly sharply?
16934.e: The standard container, used by Malcolm McLean from 1956, made reloading faster and cheaper. It is seen as the technical basis of today’s globalisation.
16934.m: The container made transporting goods around the world cheap and fast.

16935.q: Where does the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF) traditionally take place?
16935.e: The WEF was founded by Klaus Schwab in 1971 and is based in Cologny near Geneva. Its annual meeting traditionally takes place in Davos.
16935.m: The World Economic Forum meets every year in Davos.

a: Moving parts of a company abroad
16936.e: In offshoring, companies move production or services to other countries, often because of lower costs. It is a typical feature of economic globalisation.
16936.m: Offshoring means that companies move work abroad.

16937.q: Which two republics declared their independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991?
16937.e: Slovenia and Croatia declared themselves independent on 25 June 1991. The Ten-Day War in Slovenia and the war in Croatia followed.
16937.m: The break-up of Yugoslavia began with the declarations of independence in 1991.

16938.q: Which long-serving head of state of Yugoslavia died in 1980?
16938.e: Josip Broz Tito led Yugoslavia from 1945 until his death on 4 May 1980. After that, tensions between the republics grew.
16938.m: After Tito’s death in 1980, tensions in Yugoslavia grew.

16939.q: How many Bosniak men and boys were killed in the Srebrenica massacre in July 1995?
16939.e: In July 1995 Bosnian Serb troops under Ratko Mladić killed more than 8,000 Bosniaks. International courts classified the crime as genocide.
16939.m: The Srebrenica massacre of 1995 was classified by courts as genocide.

16940.q: Which agreement ended the Bosnian War and was signed in Paris on 14 December 1995?
16940.e: The agreement was negotiated in Dayton (USA) in November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December 1995. It divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities.
16940.m: The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War in 1995.

16941.q: In which city was the UN tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) based?
16941.e: The UN Security Council created the tribunal in 1993. It sat in The Hague and, among others, sentenced Ratko Mladić to life imprisonment in 2017.
16941.m: War crimes in Yugoslavia were tried before the UN tribunal in The Hague.

16942.q: When did NATO carry out air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the Kosovo War?
16942.e: The NATO air strikes lasted from 24 March to 10 June 1999. They took place without an explicit mandate from the UN Security Council.
16942.m: In the Kosovo War in 1999 NATO carried out air strikes for about eleven weeks.

16943.q: When did Kosovo declare its independence from Serbia?
16943.e: Kosovo’s parliament declared independence on 17 February 2008. Serbia still does not recognise it (as of 2026); Switzerland recognised Kosovo in February 2008.

16944.q: What is the name of the Swiss Army contingent that has served in KFOR in Kosovo since 1999?
16944.e: Swisscoy has been part of the international Kosovo Force KFOR since 1999. It is a voluntary peace support mission of the Swiss Army.
16944.m: Since 1999 Swisscoy has helped to keep the peace in Kosovo.

16945.q: How many planes were hijacked by terrorists on 11 September 2001?
16945.e: The attackers hijacked four passenger planes. Two hit the World Trade Center, one hit the Pentagon and one crashed in Pennsylvania.
16945.m: Four planes were hijacked on 11 September 2001.

16946.q: Which terrorist organisation was responsible for the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16946.e: The attacks were planned by al-Qaeda under Osama bin Laden. The 19 attackers belonged to this network.
16946.m: Al-Qaeda was behind the attacks of 11 September.

16947.q: How many attackers took part in the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16947.e: Nineteen men hijacked the four planes. Fifteen of them were Saudi citizens.
16947.m: Nineteen attackers carried out the attacks of 11 September.

16948.q: Where did United Airlines Flight 93 crash after passengers had fought back against the hijackers?
16948.e: Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville in Pennsylvania. Its real target is not known for certain.
16948.m: Flight 93 did not reach its target and crashed in Pennsylvania.

16949.q: Which building near Washington was hit by American Airlines Flight 77?
16949.e: Flight 77 was steered into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. People died on the plane and in the building.
16949.m: The Pentagon was also hit on 11 September 2001.

16950.q: Which clause of the NATO treaty was applied for the first time in the alliance’s history after the attacks of 11 September 2001?
a: The mutual defence clause in Article 5
16950.e: On 12 September 2001 the NATO Council declared that Article 5 applied, provided the attack came from abroad. This was confirmed on 2 October 2001; it was the first use of the mutual defence clause.
16950.m: After 11 September, NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time.

16951.q: When and where was Osama bin Laden killed by a US special forces unit?
16951.e: Bin Laden was killed on 2 May 2011 in Operation Neptune Spear in Abbottabad. He had been hiding there for years.
16951.m: Osama bin Laden was killed in Pakistan in 2011.

16952.q: According to official figures, how many people died in total in the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16952.e: Officially 2,996 people died, including the 19 attackers. Most of the victims were in the World Trade Center in New York.
16952.m: The attacks of 11 September cost about 3,000 people their lives.

16953.q: On which day did the USA and its allies begin Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan?
16953.e: On 7 October 2001 attacks on Taliban and al-Qaeda positions began. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden.
16953.m: The war in Afghanistan began on 7 October 2001.

16954.q: Which international force was created by UN Resolution 1386 in December 2001?
16954.e: The International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) was at first meant to ensure security in Kabul. From 2003 it was under NATO command.
16954.m: ISAF was the international security force in Afghanistan.

16955.q: Who was chosen as head of the interim government at the Afghanistan conference on the Petersberg near Bonn at the end of 2001?
16955.e: The Petersberg conference formed an interim government at the end of 2001. Hamid Karzai was put at its head and later elected President.
16955.m: Hamid Karzai led Afghanistan after the fall of the Taliban.

16956.q: Which group took Kabul without a fight on 13 November 2001?
16956.e: The Afghan Northern Alliance entered Kabul in November 2001 after the Taliban had withdrawn. It was supported from the air by the USA.
16956.m: The Northern Alliance took over Kabul in November 2001.

16957.q: Between whom was the Doha Agreement concluded on 29 February 2020?
16957.e: The Doha Agreement set out the withdrawal of US troops. In return, the Taliban promised, among other things, not to give terrorist groups room to operate.
16957.m: In the Doha Agreement of 2020 the USA agreed the withdrawal with the Taliban.

16958.q: On which day did the Taliban take Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani flee?
16958.e: On 15 August 2021 the Taliban entered Kabul and Ghani left the country. This ended the government supported by Western states.
16958.m: On 15 August 2021 the Taliban took power in Kabul again.

16959.q: When did the last US soldiers leave Afghanistan?
16959.e: After an evacuation operation at Kabul airport, the last US soldiers flew out on 30 August 2021. This ended the mission of almost 20 years.
16959.m: The US military mission in Afghanistan ended in August 2021.

16960.q: What was the main task of NATO’s Resolute Support mission, which followed ISAF in Afghanistan in 2015?
a: Training and advising Afghan security forces
Guarding the border with Pakistan on its own
16960.e: After ISAF’s combat mission ended at the end of 2014, Resolute Support took over. It trained Afghan forces and ended in 2021.
16960.m: From 2015 Resolute Support was NATO’s training mission in Afghanistan.

16961.q: On which date did the Iraq War begin with attacks by the US-led coalition?
16961.e: The bombing began in the night between 19 and 20 March 2003. Ground troops then advanced quickly on Baghdad.
16961.m: The Iraq War began on 20 March 2003.

16962.q: What was the main reason the USA and Great Britain gave for attacking Iraq?
a: Its alleged possession of weapons of mass destruction
16962.e: The governments pointed above all to alleged weapons of mass destruction. Apart from old leftover stocks, no such weapons were found after the war.
16962.m: The claimed weapons of mass destruction were not found in Iraq.

16963.q: Which US Secretary of State presented alleged evidence against Iraq to the UN Security Council on 5 February 2003?
16963.e: Colin Powell presented material on alleged weapons programmes to the Security Council. Important parts of it later turned out to be false.
16963.m: Powell’s speech at the UN in 2003 is a well-known example of faulty intelligence.

16964.q: What happened to Saddam Hussein in December 2003?
a: He was captured by US troops near Tikrit
He fled into exile in Syria
He died in an air strike on Baghdad
16964.e: Saddam Hussein was captured on 13 December 2003 in a hiding place near Tikrit. He was then handed over to a special Iraqi court.
16964.m: Saddam Hussein was captured near Tikrit at the end of 2003.

16965.q: In which year was Saddam Hussein executed?
16965.e: After being sentenced on 5 November 2006, Saddam Hussein was executed on 30 December 2006.
16965.m: Saddam Hussein was executed at the end of 2006.

16966.q: Which two large EU states openly opposed the Iraq War in 2003?
16966.e: Germany and France spoke out against the war. Great Britain, Spain, Italy and Poland, on the other hand, supported the USA.
16966.m: The Iraq War divided the European states in 2003.

16967.q: In which year did the last US troops leave Iraq after the Iraq War?
16967.e: The US combat mission officially ended in August 2010. The last US soldiers left the country in December 2011 under President Obama.
16967.m: At the end of 2011 the last US troops left Iraq.

16968.q: Which terrorist militia proclaimed a “caliphate” in 2014 after conquests in Iraq and Syria?
16968.e: The so-called Islamic State conquered Mosul, among other places, in 2014 and proclaimed a caliphate. Its rise is closely linked to the instability after the Iraq War.
16968.m: Islamic State used the instability in Iraq for its rise.

16969.q: In which US market did the financial crisis begin from 2007?
a: The market for Greek government bonds
16969.e: Many home loans had been given to borrowers with poor creditworthiness. When house prices fell, the securities bundled from them lost much of their value.
16969.m: The financial crisis began with bad mortgage loans in the USA.

16970.q: Which US investment bank went bankrupt on 15 September 2008?
16970.e: Lehman Brothers filed for insolvency on 15 September 2008 after no government rescue came. Afterwards lending between banks almost collapsed worldwide.
16970.m: The collapse of Lehman Brothers made the financial crisis dramatically worse in 2008.

16971.q: How much money did the US rescue law of October 2008 provide for stabilising the banks?
16971.e: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 had a volume of 700 billion dollars. It funded the TARP programme.
16971.m: In 2008 the USA provided about 700 billion dollars to rescue the banks.

16972.q: Which major Swiss bank was supported by the Confederation and the National Bank in October 2008?
16972.e: On 16 October 2008 the Confederation and the SNB announced a rescue package for UBS. The Confederation subscribed to mandatory convertible notes worth 6 billion francs.
16972.m: The Confederation and the National Bank supported UBS in 2008.

16973.q: What did the National Bank’s stabilisation fund take over from UBS in 2008?
a: Risky securities that were hard to sell
16973.e: In 2008 the SNB set up the StabFund, which took over illiquid and risky securities from UBS. This relieved the bank’s balance sheet without the state taking over the bank.
16973.m: The National Bank’s StabFund took over risky securities from UBS in 2008.

16974.q: Which country was the first euro country to fall into a serious debt crisis from 2010 and receive rescue loans?
16974.e: In 2010 Greece received a first aid package from euro states and the IMF. The financial crisis thus turned into the euro crisis.
16974.m: The euro crisis began with Greece in 2010.

16975.q: Which President of the European Central Bank said in July 2012 that the ECB would do “whatever it takes” to preserve the euro?
16975.e: Mario Draghi made this promise in London in July 2012. Risk premiums on government bonds in the euro area then fell clearly.
16975.m: Draghi’s promise of 2012 calmed the markets in the euro crisis.

16976.q: What does the expression “too big to fail” mean in connection with the financial crisis?
a: A bank is so important that the state cannot let it collapse
A bank is too big to grow
A state is too big to go bankrupt
A stock exchange must never be closed
16976.e: If systemically important banks collapse, they can endanger the whole economy. That is why they were given stricter rules, in Switzerland for example through the too-big-to-fail legislation.
16976.m: Systemically important banks are so important that their collapse threatens the whole economy.

16977.q: Which event on 17 December 2010 in Sidi Bouzid is seen as the trigger of the Arab Spring?
a: The self-immolation of the vegetable seller Mohamed Bouazizi
The election of a new president
16977.e: Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in protest against arbitrary treatment by the authorities. Nationwide protests in Tunisia followed.
16977.m: Mohamed Bouazizi’s act sparked the protests in Tunisia.

16978.q: Which Tunisian President fled abroad on 14 January 2011?
16978.e: After weeks of protests, Ben Ali left Tunisia on 14 January 2011. He had ruled the country since 1987.
16978.m: Ben Ali was the first ruler to be overthrown in the Arab Spring.

16979.q: Which square in Cairo became the centre of the protests against President Hosni Mubarak in 2011?
16979.e: Hundreds of thousands gathered in Tahrir Square for weeks. On 11 February 2011 Mubarak resigned after about 30 years in power.
16979.m: Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after protests in Tahrir Square.

16980.q: What did UN Security Council Resolution 1973 of 17 March 2011 make possible?
16980.e: The resolution allowed measures to protect the civilian population in Libya, including a no-fly zone. Western states then intervened militarily.
16980.m: With Resolution 1973 the UN allowed intervention in Libya in 2011.

16981.q: When and where was Muammar al-Gaddafi killed?
16981.e: Gaddafi was killed near Sirte on 20 October 2011 after being captured. This ended his rule of more than 40 years.
16981.m: Gaddafi’s rule ended with his death in October 2011.

16982.q: Who was elected Egypt’s first freely elected President in 2012 and removed by the military in 2013?
16982.e: Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood won the presidential election of 2012. In July 2013 the military removed him.
16982.m: Mohamed Morsi was Egypt’s first freely elected President.

16983.q: Which group received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its contribution to democracy in Tunisia?
16983.e: The quartet of a trade union, an employers’ federation, a human rights league and the bar association mediated in a political crisis. For this it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.
16983.m: The Tunisian Dialogue Quartet received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.

16984.q: When did the rule of Bashar al-Assad in Syria, whose government had cracked down on protests from 2011, end?
16984.e: The protests of 2011 developed into a long civil war. On 8 December 2024 Assad fled to Russia after rebels had taken Damascus.
16984.m: Assad’s rule in Syria ended in December 2024.

16985.q: What is the name of the virus that causes the disease COVID-19?
16985.e: COVID-19 is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. The first known cases appeared at the end of 2019 in Wuhan in China.
16985.m: The SARS-CoV-2 virus causes the disease COVID-19.

16986.q: On which day did the World Health Organization (WHO) classify COVID-19 as a pandemic?
16986.e: On 30 January 2020 the WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern. On 11 March 2020 it spoke of a pandemic.
16986.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020.

16987.q: When and where was the first COVID-19 case confirmed in Switzerland?
16987.e: The first case was a man in the canton of Ticino. It was confirmed on 25 February 2020.
16987.m: The first Swiss COVID-19 case was confirmed in Ticino in February 2020.

16988.q: Which level under the Epidemics Act did the Federal Council declare on 16 March 2020?
a: A state of emergency under martial law
16988.e: The Epidemics Act has a normal, a special and an extraordinary situation. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation, and in June 2020 the special situation followed again.
16988.m: In March 2020 the extraordinary situation applied in Switzerland.

16989.q: Which vaccine did Swissmedic authorise on 19 December 2020 as the first COVID-19 vaccine, for a limited time?
16989.e: On 19 December 2020 Swissmedic granted temporary authorisation for the mRNA vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech. It was the first COVID-19 vaccine authorised in Switzerland.
16989.m: The first COVID-19 vaccine authorised in Switzerland came from Pfizer and BioNTech.

16990.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the Covid-19 Act on 13 June 2021?
16990.e: The Covid-19 Act was accepted with 60.2 percent yes. The amendments in November 2021 and the extension in June 2023 were also accepted.
16990.m: Voters said yes to the Covid-19 Act three times.

16991.q: For which basic research did Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023?
a: For work that made mRNA vaccines possible
16991.e: Karikó and Weissman found out how to change mRNA so that it does not cause strong inflammation. This was a basis for the COVID-19 vaccines.
16991.m: The research of Karikó and Weissman made mRNA vaccines possible.

16992.q: When did the WHO declare the end of the global health emergency due to COVID-19?
16992.e: On 5 May 2023 the WHO lifted the international emergency. However, it stressed that the virus was still circulating.
16992.m: The WHO ended the global COVID-19 emergency in May 2023.

16993.q: Which computer network of 1969 is considered the forerunner of the internet?
16993.e: ARPANET was built from 1969 on behalf of the US Department of Defense. At first it connected a few universities and research institutes.
16993.m: The ARPANET of 1969 is the forerunner of the internet.

16994.q: At which research institution did Tim Berners-Lee develop the World Wide Web from 1989?
16994.e: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the concept at CERN in March 1989, supported by Robert Cailliau. The first website went online in 1990.
16994.m: The World Wide Web was created at CERN near Geneva.

16995.q: What happened to the World Wide Web on 30 April 1993?
a: CERN released it for free use
It was sold to a company
It was banned in Europe for the first time
16995.e: On 30 April 1993 CERN made web technology available to the public free of licence fees. This helped it spread quickly around the world.
16995.m: Since 1993 the World Wide Web has been free for everyone to use.

16996.q: In which year did Apple present the first iPhone?
16996.e: Steve Jobs presented the iPhone in January 2007. With its touchscreen and mobile internet access, it greatly changed the way people use digital services.
16996.m: The triumph of smartphones began with the iPhone in 2007.

16997.q: Since when has the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applied?
16997.e: The GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018. It also applies to Swiss companies that process data of people in the EU.
16997.m: Since 2018 the GDPR has governed data protection in the EU.

16998.q: When did Switzerland’s revised Data Protection Act come into force?
16998.e: The fully revised Data Protection Act has applied since 1 September 2023. It brought Swiss data protection up to date with digital developments and European standards.
16998.m: The new Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.

16999.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the law on a state e-ID on 28 September 2025?
a: Narrowly accepted with about 50.4 percent yes
Clearly rejected with about 64 percent no
Clearly accepted with about 64 percent yes
Narrowly rejected with about 50.4 percent no
16999.e: A first e-ID proposal with private providers had been rejected on 7 March 2021 with about 64 percent no. The new proposal with a state e-ID was narrowly accepted on 28 September 2025 with 50.4 percent yes (as of 2026).
16999.m: In 2025 Switzerland narrowly said yes to a state e-ID.

17000.q: Under which name did Facebook start at Harvard University in February 2004?
17000.e: Mark Zuckerberg founded the network in 2004 with fellow students such as Eduardo Saverin and Dustin Moskovitz. At first it was called “Thefacebook”; in 2005 the name was shortened to “Facebook”.
17000.m: Facebook started in 2004 under the name “Thefacebook”.

17001.q: What has the Facebook company been called since it was renamed in October 2021?
17001.e: On 28 October 2021 the company announced it was changing its name to Meta. It owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, among others.
17001.m: The Facebook company has been called Meta since 2021.

17002.q: Which entrepreneur took over the short message service Twitter at the end of October 2022?
17002.e: Elon Musk took over Twitter at the end of October 2022. In July 2023 the service was renamed X.
17002.m: Twitter has belonged to Elon Musk since 2022 and is now called X.

17003.q: Which company bought the video platform YouTube in 2006?
17003.e: YouTube was founded in 2005 and taken over by Google as early as 2006. Today it belongs to Google’s parent company Alphabet.
17003.m: YouTube has belonged to Google since 2006.

17004.q: In which 2018 scandal was data from millions of Facebook users analysed for political advertising without their knowledge?
17004.e: The firm Cambridge Analytica had obtained data from many Facebook profiles without consent and used it for political campaigns. The case became known in 2018.
17004.m: In 2018 the Cambridge Analytica scandal showed the risks in handling user data.

17005.q: Which country was the first to ban children under 16 by law from having their own accounts on major social networks (from 10 December 2025)?
17005.e: In Australia, since 10 December 2025, platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and YouTube must prevent under-16s from having an account. Companies face large fines if they break the rule.
17005.m: In 2025 Australia introduced a minimum age of 16 for social networks.

17006.q: Which Chinese company developed the platform TikTok?
17006.e: TikTok comes from the Chinese company ByteDance, which runs the sister app Douyin in China. TikTok spread internationally from 2017; for the US business a separate joint venture was formed in 2026, in which ByteDance holds only a minority.
17006.m: TikTok was developed by the Chinese company ByteDance.

17008.q: With whom did the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change share the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007?
17008.e: The IPCC and the former US Vice President Al Gore received the Nobel Peace Prize together in 2007. They were honoured for their contributions to knowledge about climate change.
17008.m: In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.

17009.q: In which city was a protocol with binding reduction targets for industrialised countries agreed in 1997?
17009.e: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 set binding targets for cutting greenhouse gases for industrialised countries for the first time. It came into force in 2005.
17009.m: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 brought the first binding climate targets.

17010.q: Which temperature target does the Paris Agreement of 2015 set?
a: Warming well below 2 degrees, ideally 1.5 degrees
Warming of no more than 3 degrees
Warming of no more than 2.5 degrees
17010.e: The agreement adopted on 12 December 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees compared with pre-industrial times. The goal is 1.5 degrees.
17010.m: The Paris Agreement aims to limit warming to 1.5 degrees.

17011.q: When did the Paris Agreement come into force?
17011.e: The agreement came into force on 4 November 2016 after enough states had ratified it. For Switzerland it has applied since November 2017.
17011.m: The Paris climate agreement has been in force since November 2016.

17012.q: How has the USA’s participation in the Paris Agreement developed (as of 2026)?
a: Left in 2020, rejoined in 2021, left again in 2026
The USA never joined the agreement
The USA has been a member without a break since 2016
Left in 2017 and never a member since
17012.e: The first withdrawal took effect on 4 November 2020, and from 19 February 2021 the USA was a member again. After a new declaration of withdrawal on 20 January 2025, the USA has no longer been a party since 27 January 2026.
17012.m: The USA has left the Paris Agreement twice, most recently with effect in 2026.

17013.q: Which target is contained in the Climate and Innovation Act that Switzerland approved on 18 June 2023?
a: Net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050
A ban on all petrol cars by 2030
17013.e: The act was approved with 59.1 percent yes and has been in force since 1 January 2025. It states that Switzerland should reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 (as of 2026).
17013.m: Under the Climate Act, Switzerland aims to reach net zero by 2050.

17014.q: What did the European Court of Human Rights decide on 9 April 2024 in the case of the KlimaSeniorinnen (Senior Women for Climate Protection) against Switzerland?
a: Switzerland had violated the right to private and family life
Switzerland must adopt the EU climate targets
Switzerland must shut down its nuclear power stations
17014.e: The court found a violation of Article 8 of the ECHR because Switzerland had done too little against climate change. Article 6 was also judged to have been violated.
17014.m: In the KlimaSeniorinnen case in 2024, the Court of Human Rights ruled against Switzerland.

17015.q: Who proposed a test in 1950 to check whether a machine can think like a human?
17015.e: In 1950 Alan Turing described the so-called imitation game. It became known as the Turing test.
17015.m: The Turing test goes back to Alan Turing in 1950.

17016.q: At which conference in 1956 was the term “artificial intelligence” established as a field of research?
17016.e: The Dartmouth Conference of 1956 was co-organised by John McCarthy. The term “artificial intelligence” comes from the proposal for this conference.
17016.m: The Dartmouth Conference of 1956 is seen as the birth of AI research.

17017.q: Which computer beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997?
17017.e: In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue won a six-game match against Kasparov. It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost to a computer in this way.
17017.m: In 1997 Deep Blue beat a reigning world chess champion for the first time.

17018.q: Which DeepMind program won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol in March 2016?
17018.e: AlphaGo won the match in Seoul 4 to 1. Because of the huge number of possible moves, Go was considered especially difficult for computers.
17018.m: In 2016 AlphaGo beat one of the world’s best Go players.

17019.q: When did OpenAI release the chatbot ChatGPT to the general public?
17019.e: ChatGPT was made freely available on 30 November 2022. It is based on a large language model with a transformer architecture.
17019.m: ChatGPT has been available to the public since the end of 2022.

17020.q: On what principle does the EU’s AI Act (in force since 1 August 2024) classify AI systems?
a: By the risk to people and fundamental rights
17020.e: The regulation distinguishes between unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk. The higher the risk, the stricter the obligations.
17020.m: The EU’s AI Act regulates AI systems according to their risk.

17021.q: Which two researchers received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for the foundations of machine learning with neural networks?
17021.e: Hopfield and Hinton were honoured for fundamental discoveries about artificial neural networks. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Hassabis and Jumper, among others, for AlphaFold.
17021.m: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured pioneers of neural networks.

17022.e: Asia is the biggest continent. It has the most area.
17022.m: Asia is the biggest continent on Earth.

17023.e: Australia is the smallest continent. Most of it belongs to the country of Australia.

17024.e: A continent is a very large landmass. There are often many countries on it.
17024.m: A continent is a huge piece of land.

17025.e: The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean. Its name means “peaceful ocean”.
17025.m: The Pacific is the biggest ocean on Earth.

17026.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and America?
17026.e: The Atlantic separates Europe and Africa from America. Ships need many days to cross it.
17026.m: The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.

17027.q: What does the water in the ocean taste like?
17027.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. That is why you cannot drink it.
17027.m: The water in the ocean is salty.

17028.q: What colour are oceans usually on maps?
17028.e: On maps and globes, water is almost always drawn in blue. That way you recognise it at once.
17028.m: Oceans are usually blue on maps.

17029.q: Which country is the biggest in the world?
17029.e: Russia has the largest area of all countries. It lies in Europe and in Asia.
17029.m: Russia is the biggest country in the world by area.

17030.q: Which country is the smallest in the world?
17030.e: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre. The Pope lives there.
17030.m: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

17031.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is very small and lies to the east?
17031.e: Liechtenstein lies between Switzerland and Austria. It is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
17031.m: Liechtenstein is a small neighbouring country of Switzerland.

17032.q: What does the Swiss flag look like?
17032.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is square.
17032.m: The Swiss flag has a white cross on a red background.

17033.q: Which country has a white flag with a red circle?
17033.e: The red circle on the Japanese flag stands for the sun. Japan is also called the “Land of the Rising Sun”.
17033.m: The flag of Japan shows a red circle on white.

17034.q: How many stars does the flag of the USA have?
17034.e: Each of the 50 stars stands for one state of the USA. The 13 stripes are a reminder of the first colonies.
17034.m: The flag of the USA has 50 stars.

17035.q: In which city is the seat of the Swiss government?
17035.e: The Federal Council and Parliament work in Bern. Bern is called the federal city.

17036.q: What is the capital of Austria?
17036.e: Vienna is the capital and the largest city of Austria. The famous Schönbrunn Palace is there.
17036.m: Vienna is the capital of Austria.

17037.q: What is the capital of Spain?
17037.e: Madrid lies roughly in the middle of Spain. It is the largest city in the country.
17037.m: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

17038.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17038.e: Tokyo is the capital of Japan. A great many people live in the Tokyo region.
17038.m: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

17039.q: What money do people pay with in Switzerland?
17039.e: In Switzerland people pay with francs and centimes (Rappen). One franc has 100 Rappen.
17039.m: In Switzerland you pay with francs.

17040.q: What is the capital of Germany?
17040.e: Berlin is the capital and the largest city of Germany. The Brandenburg Gate is there.
17040.m: Berlin is the capital of Germany.

17041.q: What is the highest mountain in Germany called?
17041.e: The Zugspitze is about 2960 metres high. It lies on the border with Austria.
17041.m: The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.

17042.q: In which direction is Germany from Switzerland?
17042.e: Germany lies north of Switzerland. Basel and Schaffhausen are close to the border.
17042.m: Germany lies to the north of Switzerland.

17043.q: How many federal states does Germany have?
17043.e: Germany is divided into 16 federal states, for example Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

17044.q: In which city is the Eiffel Tower?
17044.e: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris. It is made of iron and is about 330 metres high.
17044.m: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris.

17045.q: What colours is the flag of France?
17045.e: The French flag has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red.
17045.m: The flag of France is blue, white and red.

17046.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the west of Switzerland?
17046.e: France lies to the west of Switzerland. The city of Geneva is right on the border with France.
17046.m: France lies to the west of Switzerland.

17047.q: What does Italy look like on the map?
17047.e: Italy is long and narrow and looks like a boot. The toe points into the Mediterranean.
17047.m: On the map, Italy looks like a boot.

17048.q: What is the capital of Italy?
17048.e: Rome is the capital of Italy. The Colosseum is there.
17048.m: Rome is the capital of Italy.

17049.q: Which dish originally comes from Italy?
17049.e: Pizza as we know it comes from Naples in Italy.

17050.q: In which Italian city do people travel by boat instead of by car?
17050.e: Venice is built on lots of small islands. Instead of roads there are canals and narrow lanes, and people travel by boat and gondola.
17050.m: In Venice people travel by boat on canals.

17051.q: Which sea lies to the south of Europe?
17051.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe and Africa. Many people go on beach holidays there.
17051.m: The Mediterranean lies to the south of Europe.

17052.q: Which mountain range forms a border between Europe and Asia?
17052.e: The Urals are a long mountain range in Russia. They are seen as the border between Europe and Asia.
17052.m: The Urals separate Europe and Asia.

17053.q: What is the money that people pay with in many countries of Europe called?
17053.e: Many countries in Europe share the euro as their money. Switzerland is not one of them.
17053.m: In many countries of Europe people pay with euros.

17054.q: What is the highest mountain in Africa called?
17054.e: Kilimanjaro is in Tanzania and is almost 5900 metres high. There is snow at the top, even though it is hot at the bottom.
17054.m: Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.

17055.q: In which African country are the famous pyramids of Giza?
17055.e: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt. They were built more than 4000 years ago.
17055.m: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt.

17056.q: Which big river flows through Egypt?
17056.e: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world. It flows through Egypt into the Mediterranean.

17057.q: Which animal lives in the wild in Africa?
17057.e: Giraffes live in the African savannah. With their long necks they eat leaves from tall trees.
17057.m: Giraffes live in the wild in Africa.

17058.q: In which country is the Great Wall?
17058.e: The Great Wall of China is a very long structure in China. It was built for protection against enemies.
17058.m: The Great Wall is in China.

17059.q: In which country do giant pandas live in the wild?
17059.e: Giant pandas live in mountain forests in China. They mainly eat bamboo.
17059.m: Giant pandas live in the wild in China.

17060.q: Which country has had the most inhabitants in the world since 2023?
17060.e: Since 2023, more people have lived in India than in any other country. There are over 1.4 billion (as of 2025).
17060.m: India has had the most inhabitants since 2023.

17061.q: On which continent do the most people live?
17061.e: More than half of all people live in Asia. Some very populous countries are there.

17062.q: Which two parts make up America?
17062.e: America is made up of North America and South America. Central America lies in between.
17062.m: America is made up of North America and South America.

17063.q: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
17063.e: The Statue of Liberty stands on a small island near New York. France gave it to the USA as a gift.
17063.m: The Statue of Liberty is in New York.

17064.q: Which is the biggest country in South America?
17064.e: Brazil is the biggest country in South America. People there speak Portuguese.
17064.m: Brazil is the biggest country in South America.

17065.q: Who came to America by ship in 1492?
17065.e: Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492. He reached islands off America.

17066.q: Which animal carries its baby in a pouch and lives in Australia?
17066.e: The kangaroo is a marsupial. The baby grows up in its mother's pouch.
17066.m: The kangaroo lives in Australia and has a pouch.

17067.q: Which animal sleeps a lot and eats eucalyptus leaves?
17067.e: The koala lives in Australia in eucalyptus trees. It sleeps almost all day.

17068.q: What is the capital of Australia?
17068.e: Many people think of Sydney, but the capital is Canberra. Sydney is the biggest city.
17068.m: Canberra is the capital of Australia.

17069.q: What is the famous red rock in Australia called?
17069.e: Uluru is a huge red rock in the middle of Australia. It is sacred to the Aboriginal people.
17069.m: Uluru is a big red rock in Australia.

17070.q: What is Antarctica almost completely covered with?
17070.e: Antarctica is almost completely covered by a thick layer of ice. In many places the ice is kilometres thick.
17070.m: Antarctica is covered with thick ice.

17071.e: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim well. Many species live in the south, for example in Antarctica.

17072.q: Who lives in Antarctica for a while?
17072.e: There are no towns in Antarctica. Researchers live there in stations and study the ice and weather.
17072.m: Researchers live in stations in Antarctica.

17073.q: What is the weather usually like in Antarctica?
17073.e: Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth. Temperatures below minus 80 degrees have been measured there.
17073.m: It is very cold in Antarctica.

17074.q: What is the highest mountain in the world called?
17074.e: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas. It is about 8849 metres high.
17074.m: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

17075.q: Which pointed mountain stands near Zermatt?
17075.e: The Matterhorn is in Valais near Zermatt. Its pyramid shape is known all over the world.

17076.q: What do you call the highest point of a mountain?
17076.e: The summit is the very top of a mountain. There is often a summit cross there.
17076.m: The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.

17077.q: What do you call the place where a river begins?
17077.e: At the source, the water often comes out of the ground. From there it flows on as a stream.
17077.m: A river begins at its source.

17078.e: The Rhine flows through Basel and then on into Germany. Basel has a Rhine port.

17079.q: Which sea does the Rhone flow into?
17079.e: The Rhone begins at the Rhone Glacier in Valais. It flows through France into the Mediterranean.
17079.m: The Rhone flows into the Mediterranean.

17080.q: Which river flows through the city of Bern?
17080.e: In Bern the Aare makes a big loop around the old town. In summer lots of people swim in it.

17081.q: Which lake is the largest in Switzerland?
17081.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland. Part of it belongs to France.
17081.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.

17082.q: Which lake do Switzerland, Germany and Austria all border?
17082.e: Lake Constance lies between three countries. Towns such as Konstanz and Bregenz are on its shores.

17083.q: Which lake is the city of Lucerne on?
17083.e: Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne. Many boats sail across the lake from there.

17084.q: What kind of water do most lakes have?
17084.e: Most lakes are filled with fresh water. There is hardly any salt in it.

17085.q: Does Switzerland have a coastline on the sea?
17085.e: Switzerland is a landlocked country. That means it has no access to the sea.
17085.m: Switzerland is not by the sea.

17086.q: In which sea can you float on top almost without swimming?
17086.e: The Dead Sea is extremely salty. All that salt holds your body up, so you float on top.
17086.m: In the Dead Sea you float on top because of the salt.

17087.q: What is it called when the sea goes back from the beach?
17087.e: At low tide the water level drops and the beach gets wider. At high tide the water rises again.
17087.m: At low tide the sea goes back.

a: Land surrounded by water on all sides
17088.e: An island is a piece of land completely surrounded by water. You can often only reach it by ship or plane.
17088.m: An island is surrounded by water on all sides.

17089.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
17089.e: Greenland is the largest island in the world. Most of it is covered with ice.
17089.m: Greenland is the largest island in the world.

17090.q: Which large island lies off the east coast of Africa?
17090.e: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean off Africa. Lemurs live there.
17090.m: Madagascar lies off the coast of Africa.

17091.e: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and belongs to Italy. The volcano Etna is there.
17091.m: Sicily is an island of Italy.

17092.q: Which animal often carries loads in the desert?
17092.e: Camels can go a long time without water. That is why they are good pack animals in the desert.
17092.m: The camel is a pack animal in the desert.

17093.q: What do you call a place with water and palm trees in the desert?
17093.e: In an oasis there is water from the ground. That is why plants such as date palms grow there.
17093.m: An oasis is a place with water in the desert.

17094.q: What is there very little of in a desert?
17094.e: It hardly ever rains in the desert. That is why only a few plants grow there.
17094.m: It rains very little in the desert.

17095.q: What is the largest rainforest in the world called?
17095.e: The Amazon rainforest is in South America. It is the largest rainforest on Earth.
17095.m: The Amazon rainforest is the largest rainforest.

17096.q: What is the weather like in the tropical rainforest?
17096.e: It is warm all year in the tropical rainforest. It rains almost every day.
17096.m: The tropical rainforest is warm and wet.

17097.q: Which animal lives in the rainforest?
17097.e: Very many kinds of animals live in the rainforest. Colourful parrots live high up in the trees.

17098.e: People cut down trees for wood, fields and pastures. So a lot of rainforest disappears every year.
17098.m: Rainforests are getting smaller because trees are cut down.

17099.q: Which large predator lives near the North Pole?
17099.e: Polar bears live in the Arctic around the North Pole. They mainly hunt seals.
17099.m: Polar bears live in the Arctic.

17100.q: What do you stand on at the North Pole?
17100.e: There is no land at the North Pole. A layer of ice floats on the sea there.
17100.m: At the North Pole you stand on ice over the sea.

17101.q: Which way does the needle of a compass point?
17101.e: The compass needle is magnetic and points north. That is how you find your way.

17102.q: On which continent is the South Pole?
17102.e: The South Pole lies in the middle of the continent of Antarctica. There are no towns and no trees there.
17102.m: The South Pole is in Antarctica.

17103.q: Who was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911?
17103.e: The Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole with dog sleds in December 1911. The Briton Robert Scott got there about a month later.
17103.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911.

17104.q: Roughly how long does it stay dark at the South Pole in winter?
17104.e: At the South Pole the sun does not rise for about half a year in winter. In summer, on the other hand, it shines non-stop for about half a year.
17104.m: At the South Pole the winter night lasts about half a year.

17105.e: A globe shows the Earth as a small ball. That way you can see countries and seas in their correct positions.
17105.m: A globe is a model of the Earth.

17106.e: The Earth is round like a ball. That is why a globe is also shaped like a sphere.
17106.m: A globe is shaped like a sphere.

17107.q: What is the line that runs around the middle of the globe called?
17107.e: The equator divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half. In lowlands near the equator it is warm all year.
17107.m: The equator runs around the middle of the Earth.

17108.q: What does a world map show?
17108.e: A world map shows all the continents and seas on a flat sheet.
17108.m: A world map shows the whole Earth on a flat sheet.

17109.q: What do you call a book with lots of maps?
17109.e: In an atlas you find maps of countries, continents and the whole world.
17109.m: A book with lots of maps is called an atlas.

17110.q: Which compass direction is at the top of most maps?
17110.e: On most maps north is at the top and south at the bottom. East is on the right, west on the left.
17110.m: On most maps north is at the top.

17111.q: Which country lies entirely in Europe and is the largest by area?
17111.e: Ukraine is about 600,000 km² in size. Russia is bigger, but most of it lies in Asia.
17111.m: Ukraine is the largest country that lies entirely in Europe.

17112.q: Which of these countries does not border Switzerland?
17112.e: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. Belgium lies further to the north-west.

17113.q: Which country in the European Union has the most inhabitants?
17113.e: Germany has over 80 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That makes it the most populous country in the EU.
17113.m: Germany is the most populous country in the EU.

17114.q: Which is the smallest country in the European Union by area?
17114.e: Malta is an island state in the Mediterranean and only about 316 km² in size. Luxembourg, at around 2,600 km², is much bigger.
17114.m: Malta is the smallest country in the EU.

17115.q: What is the capital of Portugal?
17115.e: Lisbon lies where the Tagus flows into the Atlantic. Porto is the second largest city in Portugal.
17115.m: The capital of Portugal is Lisbon.

17116.q: What is the capital of Poland?
17116.e: Warsaw lies on the Vistula and is the largest city in Poland. Kraków was a royal city for a long time.
17116.m: The capital of Poland is Warsaw.

17117.q: What is the capital of Croatia?
17117.e: Zagreb lies inland in the north of Croatia. Split and Dubrovnik are well-known cities on the Adriatic coast.
17117.m: The capital of Croatia is Zagreb.

17118.q: Officially, Switzerland has no capital. What is Bern called instead?
17118.e: The Federal Council and the Federal Assembly have their seat in Bern. But the Federal Constitution names no capital, so people speak of the federal city.

17119.q: Which has been the largest country in Africa by area since 2011?
17119.e: When South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011, Algeria, at around 2.4 million km², became the largest country in Africa. Much of it is desert.
17119.m: Algeria is the largest country in Africa.

17120.q: Which country in Africa has the most inhabitants?
17120.e: Nigeria in West Africa has over 200 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That means about one in six people in Africa lives there.
17120.m: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa.

17121.q: Which country is Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, in?
17121.e: Kilimanjaro is about 5,895 m high and lies in north-eastern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya. Its highest peak is the volcano Kibo, which has been dormant for a long time.

17122.q: Which country is completely surrounded by the territory of South Africa?
17122.e: Lesotho is an enclave and lies entirely inside South Africa. It is a mountainous country with high valleys.
17122.m: Lesotho lies in the middle of South Africa.

17123.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17123.e: Tokyo lies on the main island of Honshu. Kyoto was the imperial city for over 1,000 years.
17123.m: The capital of Japan is Tokyo.

17124.q: Which country lies entirely in Asia and is the largest by area?
17124.e: China is about 9.6 million km² in size. Russia is bigger, but part of it lies in Europe.
17124.m: China is the largest country that lies entirely in Asia.

17125.q: Which island state in South-East Asia is made up of around 17,000 islands?
17125.e: Indonesia is the largest island state in the world. Among the best-known islands are Java, Bali and Sumatra.
17125.m: Indonesia is the largest island state on Earth.

17126.q: Which landlocked country lies between Russia and China?
17126.e: Mongolia borders only Russia and China and has no access to the sea. A large part of the country is steppe and the Gobi Desert.
17126.m: Mongolia is squeezed in between Russia and China.

17127.q: Which is the largest country in South America by area?
17127.e: Brazil is about 8.5 million km² in size. It takes up almost half the area of South America.
17127.m: Brazil is the largest country in South America.

17128.q: What is the capital of Canada?
17128.e: Ottawa is in the province of Ontario. Toronto is the largest city in Canada, but not the capital.
17128.m: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

17129.q: Which language is the official language of Brazil?
17129.e: Brazil was a colony of Portugal for a long time. That is why people there speak Portuguese, while Spanish is spoken in most neighbouring countries.

17130.q: In which country is the canal that links the Atlantic with the Pacific in Central America?
17130.e: The Panama Canal opened in 1914 and is about 82 km long. Ships no longer have to sail round the southern tip of South America.
17130.m: The Panama Canal links two oceans.

17131.q: Which mountain range is seen as the border between Europe and Asia?
17131.e: The Urals stretch about 2,500 km from north to south in Russia. They are usually used as the border between the two continents.
17131.m: The Urals separate Europe from Asia.

17132.q: Which mountain range forms the border between France and Spain?
17132.e: The Pyrenees reach from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. The tiny country of Andorra lies in the middle of these mountains.
17132.m: The Pyrenees lie between France and Spain.

17133.q: Which large mountain range stretches across western North America from Canada into the USA?
17133.e: The Rocky Mountains are over 4,000 km long. Well-known national parks such as Yellowstone are in these mountains.
17133.m: The Rocky Mountains are in western North America.

17134.q: Which mountain range lies in north-western Africa, mainly in Morocco?
17134.e: The Atlas Mountains run through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. They separate the Mediterranean coast from the Sahara.
17134.m: The Atlas Mountains are in north-western Africa.

17135.q: What is the highest mountain in the Alps called?
17135.e: Mont Blanc is about 4,806 m high. It lies on the border between France and Italy.
17135.m: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps.

17136.q: What is the highest peak in Switzerland called?
17136.e: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif in Valais is 4,634 m high. It is named after the Swiss general Guillaume-Henri Dufour.
17136.m: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland.

17137.q: How many countries have a share of the Alps?
17137.e: The Alps lie in France, Monaco, Italy, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. That makes eight countries.

17138.q: How high is Mount Everest according to the 2020 measurement?
17138.e: Nepal and China measured Mount Everest again together in 2020. The result was 8,848.86 m, rounded to 8,849 m.
17138.m: Mount Everest is about 8,849 m high.

17139.q: How many mountains on Earth are higher than 8,000 m?
17139.e: There are 14 eight-thousanders in the world. All of them are in the Himalayas or the neighbouring Karakoram in Asia.

17140.q: On the border of which two countries is Mount Everest?
17140.e: The summit lies exactly on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. It can be climbed from both sides.
17140.m: Mount Everest lies between Nepal and China.

17141.q: Who were the first people proven to reach the summit of Mount Everest, in 1953?
17141.e: On 29 May 1953, the New Zealander Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit. They were part of a British expedition.
17141.m: Hillary and Tenzing were the first to climb Everest, in 1953.

17142.q: What does the name “Himalaya” mean when translated from Sanskrit?
17142.e: The word is made of “hima” for snow and “alaya” for home. “Roof of the world”, on the other hand, is a nickname for the Tibetan Plateau.

17143.q: Roughly how far do the Andes in South America stretch from north to south?
17143.e: The Andes run along the west coast of South America for about 7,500 km from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego. They are seen as the longest mountain range above sea level.
17143.m: The Andes are the longest mountain range on land.

17144.q: What is the highest mountain in the Andes and in all of the Americas called?
17144.e: Aconcagua in Argentina is about 6,961 m high. It is the highest mountain outside Asia.
17144.m: Aconcagua is the highest mountain in the Americas.

17145.q: What is the famous Inca ruined city high in the Andes of Peru called?
17145.e: Machu Picchu was built by the Incas in the 15th century and lies at around 2,400 m above sea level. Chichén Itzá and Tikal are Maya cities.
17145.m: Machu Picchu is an Inca city in Peru.

17146.q: Which large lake lies in the Andes on the border between Peru and Bolivia?
17146.e: Lake Titicaca lies at around 3,800 m above sea level. It is seen as the highest large navigable body of water in the world.
17146.m: Lake Titicaca lies high in the Andes.

17147.q: Which sea does the Nile flow into?
17147.e: The Nile reaches the sea in Egypt with a large delta. A great many people live in the fertile Nile Delta.
17147.m: The Nile ends in the Mediterranean.

17148.q: In which city do the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet?
17148.e: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan. From there the river flows on northwards as the Nile.
17148.m: The White Nile and Blue Nile join in Khartoum.

17149.q: From which large lake in East Africa does the White Nile flow out?
17149.e: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa. It lies between Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.
17149.m: The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria.

17150.q: Which large reservoir was created in Egypt by the Aswan Dam?
17150.e: The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970. It dams the Nile to form Lake Nasser and protects the country from floods.
17150.m: Lake Nasser is a reservoir on the Nile.

17151.q: Which river carries the most water of all the rivers in the world?
17151.e: On average the Amazon carries over 200,000 m³ of water per second into the sea. That is more than the next seven largest rivers put together.
17151.m: The Amazon is the river with the most water on Earth.

17152.q: Which sea does the Amazon flow into?
17152.e: The Amazon flows east right across South America. It reaches the sea in Brazil through a huge estuary.
17152.m: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic.

17153.q: In which country does the Amazon begin?
17153.e: The headwaters of the Amazon rise high in the Andes of Peru. From there the water flows east.

17154.q: In which country is most of the Amazon rainforest?
17154.e: Around 60 percent of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil. It is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.
17154.m: Most of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil.

17155.q: In which mountains does the Danube begin?
17155.e: At Donaueschingen, the streams Brigach and Breg from the Black Forest flow together. From there the river is called the Danube.
17155.m: The Danube begins in the Black Forest.

17156.q: Which sea does the Danube flow into?
17156.e: The Danube reaches the sea on the border of Romania and Ukraine. There it forms a large delta with many birds.
17156.m: The Danube flows into the Black Sea.

17157.q: How many countries does the Danube flow through?
17157.e: The Danube flows through or along Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine. No other river in the world touches so many countries.

17158.q: Which of these capital cities does the Danube not flow through?
17158.e: The Vltava flows through Prague. The capitals Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade are on the Danube.
17158.m: The Danube flows through four capital cities.

17159.q: Which river from the Engadine carries water from Switzerland into the Danube?
17159.e: The Inn rises in the Upper Engadine and flows through Austria to Germany. At Passau it flows into the Danube.
17159.m: The Inn flows from the Engadine to the Danube.

17160.q: In which canton does the Rhine begin?
17160.e: The Anterior Rhine starts at Lake Toma in Graubünden. At Reichenau the Anterior and Posterior Rhine flow together.

17161.q: Which sea does the Rhine flow into?
17161.e: The Rhine flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands. The large port of Rotterdam lies where it reaches the sea.
17161.m: The Rhine ends in the North Sea.

17162.q: Near which town are the Rhine Falls?
17162.e: The Rhine Falls are at Neuhausen am Rheinfall, right next to Schaffhausen. They are among the largest waterfalls in Europe.
17162.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

17163.q: Near which Swiss city are the Rhine ports from which cargo ships sail to the North Sea?
17163.e: The Swiss Rhine ports are at Basel. From there cargo ships travel along the Rhine to the North Sea.
17163.m: In Basel, Switzerland has access to the sea via the Rhine.

17164.q: Which lake does the Rhine flow through between Switzerland, Austria and Germany?
17164.e: The Alpine Rhine flows into Lake Constance in Vorarlberg (Austria), and the Rhine leaves the lake again at Stein am Rhein. Lake Constance borders three countries.
17164.m: The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.

17165.q: Which strait links the Mediterranean with the Atlantic?
17165.e: The Strait of Gibraltar lies between Spain and Morocco. At its narrowest point it is only about 14 km wide.
17165.m: At Gibraltar the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.

17166.q: Which canal links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea?
17166.e: The Suez Canal in Egypt opened in 1869. Since then ships from Europe to Asia no longer have to sail round Africa.
17166.m: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

17167.q: Which is the largest island in the Mediterranean?
17167.e: Sicily belongs to Italy and is about 25,700 km² in size. The volcano Etna is on the island.
17167.m: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean.

17168.q: How many continents does the Mediterranean border?
17168.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe to the north, Africa to the south and Asia to the east. Its name means “sea in the middle of the lands”.

17169.q: Which ocean is the second largest on Earth?
17169.e: The Atlantic covers about a fifth of the Earth's surface. It lies between America to the west and Europe and Africa to the east.
17169.m: The Atlantic is the second largest ocean.

17170.q: Which warm ocean current gives western Europe a mild climate?
17170.e: The Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic to Europe. That is why winters there are milder than in Canada at the same latitude.
17170.m: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe.

17171.q: Which island country lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
17171.e: In Iceland the North American and Eurasian plates drift apart. That is why there are many volcanoes and hot springs there.
17171.m: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

17172.q: Which group of islands in the middle of the Atlantic belongs to Portugal?
17172.e: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Portugal. The Canary Islands belong to Spain.
17172.m: The Azores are Portuguese islands in the Atlantic.

17173.q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
17173.e: The Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface. It is bigger than all the land on Earth put together.
17173.m: The Pacific is the largest ocean.

17174.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point in the Mariana Trench?
17174.e: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is just under 11,000 m deep. Even Mount Everest would disappear completely inside it.
17174.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest point in the oceans.

17176.q: Where does the Pacific get its name from?
a: from the name of a king
17176.e: In 1520 the seafarer Ferdinand Magellan called the sea “Mar Pacífico” because it was calm during his voyage. Pacífico means peaceful.
17176.m: The name Pacific means the peaceful one.

17177.q: Which US state is made up of islands in the middle of the Pacific?
17177.e: Hawaii lies about 3,800 km off the coast of North America. The islands were formed by volcanoes.
17177.m: Hawaii is a US island state in the Pacific.

17178.q: Which island country is made up of around 1,200 flat coral islands in the Indian Ocean?
17178.e: The Maldives lie south-west of India. Most of the islands rise only a little above sea level.
17178.m: The Maldives are made up of many flat coral islands.

17179.q: Which large island off the east coast of Africa lies in the Indian Ocean?
17179.e: Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world. Many animals live there that are found only on this island, such as lemurs.
17179.m: Madagascar lies off the east coast of Africa.

17180.q: What is the wind over the Indian Ocean called that changes direction with the seasons and brings rainy seasons to South Asia?
17180.e: In summer the monsoon blows from the sea onto the land and brings heavy rain. In winter it blows the other way and it is dry.
17180.m: The monsoon brings South Asia its rainy season.

17181.q: Off which island did an undersea earthquake set off a devastating tsunami in the Indian Ocean in December 2004?
17181.e: The earthquake off the northern tip of Sumatra on 26 December 2004 was one of the strongest ever measured. The waves hit coasts in many countries around the Indian Ocean.
17181.m: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra set off a huge tsunami in 2004.

17182.q: Ideally, how many degrees of longitude does one time zone cover?
17182.e: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. 360 divided by 24 is 15 degrees per hour.
17182.m: One hour of time difference equals 15 degrees of longitude.

17183.q: Through which part of London does the prime meridian run?
17183.e: In 1884 the prime meridian was set through the Greenwich observatory. Lines of longitude are counted east and west from there.
17183.m: The prime meridian runs through Greenwich.

17184.q: What changes when you cross the International Date Line?
17184.e: The date line runs roughly along the 180th line of longitude through the Pacific. If you travel west across it, you jump forward a day; if you travel east, you go back a day.
17184.m: At the date line the date changes.

17185.q: In winter it is 12 noon in Zurich (UTC+1). What time is it then in New York (UTC−5)?
17185.e: The difference is 1 minus (minus 5), so 6 hours. New York is further west, so you work out 12 minus 6 = 6 am.
17185.m: In the west it is earlier than in the east.

17186.q: During summer time, what time does Switzerland use compared with Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)?
17186.e: In summer the clocks in Switzerland are put forward one hour. This time is called Central European Summer Time.
17186.m: In summer Switzerland uses Central European Summer Time.

17187.q: Which climate zone is Switzerland in?
17187.e: Switzerland lies in the middle latitudes with four clear seasons. In the mountains, however, it is much colder than in the Central Plateau.
17187.m: Switzerland lies in the temperate zone.

17188.q: Between which lines do the tropics lie?
a: Between the two tropics of Cancer and Capricorn
Between the equator and the North Pole
Between the prime meridian and the date line
17188.e: The tropics of Cancer and Capricorn lie at about 23.4 degrees north and south. Between them, the sun is directly overhead at midday at least once a year.
17188.m: The tropics lie between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

17189.q: Which climate zone is the Sahara mainly in?
17189.e: The Sahara lies around the Tropic of Cancer. Dry air sinks there, which is why it very rarely rains.
17189.m: Many large deserts lie in the subtropics.

17190.q: What is the treeless landscape with mosses and lichens in the subpolar zone called?
17190.e: In the tundra the summer is too short and too cool for trees. Deep down, the ground often stays frozen all year.
17190.m: No trees grow in the tundra.

17191.q: Where can you see the midnight sun in summer?
a: Only on the Tropic of Cancer
17191.e: North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set for at least one day in midsummer. This is true, for example, in northern Norway.
17191.m: The midnight sun can be seen north of the Arctic Circle.

17192.q: Roughly how many people live on Earth (as of 2025)?
17192.e: According to the United Nations, the world population passed 8 billion in 2022. The number is still growing, but more slowly than before.
17192.m: About 8 billion people live on Earth.

17193.q: On which continent do about 60 percent of the world's people live?
17193.e: Asia has several countries with very large populations. That is why more than half of all people live there.

17194.q: Which country is the most densely populated in the world?
17194.e: Monaco is only about 2 km² in size but has about 38,000 inhabitants (as of 2023). That is over 18,000 people per km².
17194.m: Monaco is the most densely populated country.

17195.q: A country has 1,000,000 inhabitants and an area of 5,000 km². What is its population density?
17195.e: Population density is the number of inhabitants divided by the area. 1,000,000 divided by 5,000 is 200 inhabitants per km².
17195.m: For population density, you divide the number of inhabitants by the area.

17196.q: What was the Taj Mahal in India built as?
17196.e: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra in the 17th century for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is a mausoleum made of white marble.
17196.m: The Taj Mahal is a magnificent tomb.

17197.q: In which city is the large statue of Christ on Corcovado mountain?
17197.e: The statue “Christ the Redeemer” is about 30 m tall and was unveiled in 1931. It looks out over the city and the bay.
17197.m: The statue of Christ watches over Rio de Janeiro.

17198.q: In which country is the rock city of Petra?
17198.e: Over 2,000 years ago the Nabataeans carved buildings straight into the reddish rock. Petra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
17198.m: Petra is a rock city in Jordan.

17199.q: Which country gave the USA the Statue of Liberty in New York?
17199.e: The Statue of Liberty was unveiled in 1886 and was a gift from France to mark the friendship between the two countries. Its inner steel frame was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
17199.m: The Statue of Liberty is a gift from France.

17200.q: In which city is the opera house with sail-shaped roofs by the harbour?
17200.e: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973. It was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon.
17200.m: The famous opera house with sail roofs is in Sydney.

17201.q: Which is the largest lake on Earth by area?
17201.e: Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is a lake with no outlet to the sea. It is about 370,000 km² in size (a little more or less depending on the water level), about nine times the size of Switzerland.
17201.m: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth.

17202.q: Which lake is the deepest on Earth?
17202.e: Lake Baikal in Siberia is up to about 1,640 m deep. It holds about a fifth of the liquid fresh water on the Earth's surface.
17202.m: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world.

17203.q: Which is the largest island on Earth?
17203.e: Greenland is over 2 million km² in size and mostly covered with ice. Australia counts as a continent, not an island.
17203.m: Greenland is the largest island on Earth.

17204.q: Where is the lowest point on land?
17204.e: The shore of the Dead Sea is more than 430 m below sea level. The water is so salty that you can hardly sink in it.
17204.m: The Dead Sea is the lowest place on land.

17205.q: In which country is the highest waterfall on Earth, Angel Falls?
17205.e: Angel Falls plunge about 979 m. They are in a national park in south-eastern Venezuela.
17205.m: The highest waterfall on Earth is in Venezuela.

17206.q: What type of plate boundary is found at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
17206.e: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the plates move apart. Rising magma constantly forms new oceanic crust there.
17206.m: New ocean floor forms at divergent boundaries.

17207.q: What kind of plate boundary is the San Andreas Fault in California?
17207.e: The Pacific and North American Plates slide horizontally past each other there. Crust is neither created nor destroyed.
17207.m: At transform faults, plates slide sideways past each other.

17208.q: Why does the oceanic plate usually sink beneath the continental plate in a collision?
17208.e: Oceanic crust consists mainly of basalt and is heavier than the granitic continental crust. That is why it sinks into the Earth's mantle.
17208.m: The denser oceanic plate is subducted.

17209.q: The collision of which plates created the Himalayas?
17209.e: The Indian Plate drifted north and collided with the Eurasian Plate. The crust was compressed and folded up into the highest mountain range on Earth.
17209.m: The Himalayas are a collision range between India and Eurasia.

17210.q: Which process is the main cause of the formation of the Alps?
17210.e: The African Plate with the Adriatic promontory pushed against the Eurasian Plate. Rock nappes were stacked on top of each other, and they can be seen in the Swiss Alps today.
17210.m: The Alps are fold mountains formed by the collision of Africa and Europe.

17211.q: How are deep-sea trenches such as the Mariana Trench formed?
a: By erosion of the sea floor
17211.e: Where an oceanic plate sinks beneath another, a long, very deep trench forms. The Mariana Trench reaches a depth of around 11,000 metres.

17212.q: How is the formation of the Hawaiian island chain explained?
a: A plate moves over a hotspot
Plates slide past each other sideways
17212.e: A largely stationary mantle plume melts through the Pacific Plate moving above it. This creates volcanic islands one after another, which get older the further away they are.
17212.m: Hotspot island chains show the direction a plate is moving.

17213.q: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?
a: Belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific
Warm ocean current in the South Pacific
Belt of coral reefs in the western Pacific
Desert belt along the Pacific coast
17213.e: There are many subduction zones around the Pacific. That is why active volcanoes and strong earthquakes are so common there.
17213.m: The Pacific Ring of Fire follows the subduction zones around the Pacific.

17214.q: Who presented the theory of continental drift in 1912?
17214.e: The German meteorologist Alfred Wegener presented his idea in 1912 and published the book “The Origin of Continents and Oceans” in 1915.
17214.m: Alfred Wegener is considered the founder of the theory of continental drift.

17215.q: What is the name of the supercontinent that united almost all land masses at the end of the Palaeozoic?
17215.e: Pangaea united almost all continents in the late Palaeozoic and early Mesozoic. The name means “all the Earth”.
17215.m: Pangaea was the last supercontinent in Earth's history.

17216.q: Which fossil find especially supported Wegener's theory?
a: Mesosaurus in Africa and South America
17216.e: The small freshwater reptile Mesosaurus could not cross an ocean. Its presence on both sides of the South Atlantic suggests an earlier land connection.
17216.m: The same fossils on separate continents show they were once connected.

17217.q: What is the southern supercontinent called that was separated from the northern part when Pangaea broke up?
17217.e: Gondwana existed even before Pangaea and became its southern part. It included Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia and India, among others.
17217.m: Gondwana included today's southern continents and India.

17218.q: What do the symmetrical magnetic stripes on the sea floor on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges prove?
a: The cooling of the Earth's core
17218.e: As new crust cools, it records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at that time. Because the field keeps reversing, a mirror-image pattern of stripes forms.
17218.m: Magnetic stripe patterns prove that the ocean floor is spreading.

17219.q: Roughly how fast is the Atlantic opening?
a: A few millimetres per thousand years
17219.e: The spreading rate at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is around 2.5 centimetres per year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
17219.m: Plates move about as fast as fingernails grow.

17220.q: Roughly when did Pangaea begin to break apart?
17220.e: The break-up began at the transition from the Triassic to the Jurassic. Since then, the Atlantic, among others, has opened up.
17220.m: Pangaea broke apart in the Mesozoic around 200 million years ago.

17221.q: According to the UN, when did the world population pass the 8 billion mark?
17221.e: The United Nations chose 15 November 2022 as the symbolic day. The 7 billion mark had been reached in 2011.
17221.m: Since the end of 2022 more than 8 billion people have lived on Earth.

17222.q: With constant growth of 2 per cent a year, after roughly how many years does a population double?
17222.e: The doubling time is ln(2) divided by ln(1.02), which is about 35 years. A rule of thumb is 70 divided by the growth rate in per cent.
17222.m: You get a rough doubling time by dividing 70 by the growth rate.

17223.q: In countries with low mortality, which total fertility rate is considered the replacement level?
17223.e: On average each woman must have slightly more than two children for the parents' generation to be replaced. The extra makes up for deaths before adulthood and for the surplus of boys.
17223.m: The replacement level is around 2.1 children per woman.

17224.q: According to UN estimates, which country has been the most populous in the world since 2023?
17224.e: The UN estimated that India overtook China in 2023. Both countries each have over 1.4 billion inhabitants.
17224.m: India has replaced China as the most populous country.

17225.q: A country has a birth rate of 30 and a death rate of 10 per thousand. How big is the natural growth?
17225.e: Natural growth is the birth rate minus the death rate, so 30 minus 10 equals 20 per thousand. 20 per thousand is 2 per cent.
17225.m: Natural growth is the birth rate minus the death rate.

17226.q: Who warned in 1798 that population was growing faster than food production?
17226.e: In his “Essay on the Principle of Population”, Malthus wrote that population grows geometrically but food only arithmetically. Increases in farm production largely disproved this forecast.
17226.m: Malthus feared that population growth would lead to famines.

17227.q: In which phase of the demographic transition model does the population grow fastest?
a: When the death rate falls but the birth rate stays high
When the birth rate falls below the death rate
17227.e: Thanks to better hygiene, medicine and nutrition, mortality falls first. The birth rate adjusts only later, so a big gap opens up.
17227.m: The population grows fastest when the death rate has already fallen and the birth rate is still high.

17228.q: According to the UN, from when did more than half of the world's population first live in cities?
